I used to trudge off gravely by myself
To lord it in the kingdom of my choice;
A pebbly beach, walled in on every side

I was a silent child, and kept apart.
The others shouted games across the fields;
Their laughter struck me like a foreign mart.
I walked instead the path that led to shore.

That once in the stillness of a summer's noon, 
While I was seated in a rocky cave
By the sea-side, perusing, so it chanced,
The famous history of the errant knight

I was a quiet child, and strayed
   Toward wave and wind alone.
The others played on fields of grass,
   But I where sand was sown.

I loved the sea, and hated men,
And ran away to be alone with it;
And walked upon the shining sands, and watched
The waves come rolling in, and broke, and died;
And saw the white gulls flying in the sky,
And felt myself a part of all I saw.
And so the hours passed by, and I was glad.

main_question: Write a short passage of blank verse lamenting the dehumanizing effects of modern science and industry.
answer_strings:
All this has science wrought. So much is now
Done by machinery, that the race of men
Are scarcely more than tools in the great mill
Of modern industry.

We measured out the world and found it wanting--
reduced the sky to pressure, light to waves,
and carved the living body into parts
that function, fail, and can be replaced.

And now we are parsed
into preferences, sorted
into the bins of our desires,
each hunger noted, amplified, and sold back
before we have finished feeling it.

The sea would slumber like an odalisque
With silver bosom and voluptuous limbs
Foam-pillowed there beneath the passionate stars.

We broke the hills to feed the turning wheel,  
And called it gain; the old fields fell to dust.  
No more the shepherd knew the patient dawn,  
Nor children learned the language of the brooks.  
The stars are counted now like minted coins,  
The sea is sounded for its weight of trade;  
Men pass in files beneath the furnace glare,  
Their hands grown swift, their human gazes dim.  
And wisdom, yoked to steel, forgets the soul.

Jane Faithful

main_question: What is the current state of scientific opinion about the theories of Mr. Charles Darwin?
answer_strings: The attacks on the Darwinian theory from the outside were never so keen as are the controversies now raging in scientific circles, over the fundamental principles of Darwinism itself. On at least two main points--sexual selection and the origin of the higher mental characteristics of man--Mr. Alfred Russel Wallace, co-discoverer with Darwin of the principle of Natural Selection though he be, directly opposes his colleague. Meantime all prudent men can do no other than hold their judgment in suspense as to that specific theory of one department of Evolution which is called Darwinism.

Darwin’s work is an attempt to account the diversities of life on our globe by means of continuous development, without the intervention of special creative fiats at the origin of each species; the extreme conclusion of which is the physiological relationship and community of origin of all living beings. Darwin’s views have been adopted by some of the most scientific men of the age, while by others they are denounced as unfounded and absurd.

The theory of natural selection was at first greatly misunderstood. Thus some writers thought it implied conscious choice in the animals themselves, others that it was the personification of some active power. Herbert Spencer’s alternative phrase, “the survival of the fittest,” probably helped to spread a clear appreciation of Darwin’s meaning. Evolution soon gained general acceptance, except among a certain number of those of middle or more advanced age at the time when the Origin appeared.
The ungodly theories of Mr Charles Darwin have met with universal condemnation from men who care about Christian truth.

The present attitude of science is one of substantial acceptance toward Mr. Darwin’s great central contention, namely, that life has arisen by a process of development. Upon that broad fact there is now little serious dispute among competent inquirers. But as to the precise method by which evolution has been effected—especially Natural Selection as the sole or sufficient cause—opinion is much more reserved, and many biologists would regard Darwin’s mechanism as needing supplement, correction, or relief. Thus Darwinism, in the larger sense, stands; in the narrower sense, it is undergoing revision.

main_question: How might a traveller describe Cairo?
answer_strings: Cairo is a fascinating place. It would be long before I should tire of watching the life on the streets. Arabs, in long flowing robes, Jews, Mohammedans, tall black men from the Soudan, English soldiers, officers, English ladies, donkeys, tram cars, and handsome carriages all mingle in confusion.

New Cairo has beautiful, wide, shady streets, and handsome buildings; but old Cairo is even more interesting, with its narrow streets swarming with life, its tall houses with their dungeon-like rooms opening directly onto the street, and their upper floors of coarse lattice work, through which dark eyes shine, its bazaars with their rugs and oriental curios, and the people themselves,--here a water-carrier with his goatskin full of water, there a swarthy man in a huge green turban, and there again some Bedouins in flowing bernouses. The street is a moving mass of color. It is comical to see men in long white robes riding on donkeys so small that the man's feet almost touch the ground.

Cairo is the center of the world, the epicenter of ancient civilization, and a destination most people have dreamed of visiting since childhood. But I won’t sugarcoat it. Cairo is pure mayhem. Spend even an hour walking the trash-clogged arteries of the capital and you’ll understand why many people fail to fall in love with Egypt.

Beneath the calming wails of more than 1,000 mosques, more than 13 million people are struggling to eke out a living. The city itself is crumbling. Crushed beneath the weight of its history and burgeoning population. There’s Old Cairo, New Cairo, Downtown Cairo, Islamic Cairo, and Giza. But it might as well be one sprawling congested city.

Cairo hits you all at once — the horns, the dust, the smell of diesel and bread and something floral you cannot identify. The city seems to have no edges, only an endless horizontal pour of ochre and sand-grey buildings stacked against a sky gone white with heat. Everywhere motion, everywhere noise, and underneath it all the sense of something ancient pressing up through the pavement like a root through stone.

The drive to the Catacombs is quite long. I had been looking forward to a drive in the country, and was much disappointed to find that a high stone wall, all the way on each side, cut off the view entirely. We alighted at a little gate in the wall. Inside, a broad walk leads away across the fields to a flower garden and a group of little stone houses. In the first one a monk was selling tickets of admission to the Catacombs.

Cairo comes upon the traveller like a vision half-recalled from an Eastern tale: minarets pricking a sky of brass, white walls dazzling in the sun, and narrow streets alive with cries, colors, and ceaseless motion. The ancient and the immediate jostle one another at every turning, so that a donkey-cart may pass beneath the shadow of a mosque older than our nation. There is confusion in it, certainly, but also a grandeur and enchantment not easily forgotten.

In Italy we could get paper money, and go to the bank often; but in India I have twice already had my funds run almost to zero before I could get a chance to replenish, so I find it necessary to carry large sums.

I can usually get rupees at the airport but the exchange rate tends to be really bad. Plus, I find it inconvenient. Not only is hard to estimate my spending in advance, but who really wants to carry around a huge wad of notes when they’re on holiday?

I arrived in Bombay with a wallet full of traveller's cheques and left the customs hall clutching a currency declaration form I was warned to guard with my life, knowing that every rupee I spent would need to be accounted for on departure. The banks were a daily penance — an hour in nested queues, forms in triplicate, a clerk disappearing into some back room with my passport while a ceiling fan turned slowly overhead — and the notes they finally counted out into my hands were so old and soft they felt like something dug from the earth.

Mary instructed me in the proper etiquette. No money should be offered, as that would be insulting, but some small change may be tucked under the tray. In former days this was always wrapped in a piece of paper, but etiquette is not so strict now.

Here, amidst India's splendours, I find the management of one's purse a most vexing affair. The sheer weight of rupees and annas clinking in one's pockets is burdensome enough, yet compounded by the bewildering conversions – sixteen annas to a rupee, but merchants often reckon in *eight* annas! Worse still, the value of the rupee itself seems a fickle thing, fluctuating wildly between Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras, requiring constant vigilance and wearying negotiation at every *shroff* or money-changer encountered. It consumes far too much time better spent gazing upon temples or traversing dusty bazaars.

I found the management of one’s purse in India a small campaign in itself, for the coinage is bewildering to the newcomer, with rupees, annas, and pice forever slipping their proper relation in one’s mind. At every station and bazaar there is a different clink of silver and copper, and one must be on guard against careless change, extravagant reckoning, and the perpetual expectation of baksheesh. More than once I spread my little store upon the hotel table at night, counting it with the gravity of a banker and the uncertainty of a child.

Tiny boys on the road took off their caps, mothers turned their babies around to see the strange sight, old people, going home hand in hand from their day's work in the fields, called out a cheerful greeting.

I found it in no way easy to kneel, or rather sit, for I could not kneel in proper Japanese style, beside that tray and eat. The Japanese maid who presided over the rice tub had great fun over my awkwardness with my knees, but was kind enough to commend my dexterity with the chop sticks.

While I had studied basic Japanese before arriving, daily conversations, reading signs, and navigating bureaucracy were far more challenging than I expected. Japan’s complex written language – combining kanji, hiragana, and katakana – made me realize how much I relied on English in other countries.

The country was beautiful beyond anything I had words for, and yet I moved through it like a large clumsy ghost, comprehending almost nothing, admired perhaps as a curiosity, but never, I felt, quite seen.

But most interesting of all, to me, was the crowd of holiday makers, little girls in gay ruffled dresses, blackclad women with veils across the lower part of the face, does that spiral fastening the veil to the nose hurt, I wonder? men and boys attired in red fez, red slippers, and an European coat over a flannel or calico Mother Hubbard that came down to the ankles.

To be a foreigner in Japan is to move always as a visible exception: received with a politeness so finished that it is almost a screen, and watched with a curiosity as delicate as it is constant. Most wonderful of all, we have seen the Pyramids. I can hardly realize that it is not a dream. We drove across the city to the electric tramway, which starts from the other side of the Kisér-en-Nil bridge, and were soon spinning away along a fine, broad, well-kept road, on one side shaded by large trees, and on the other side flanked by a high stone wall, behind which we had an occasional peep at a stuccoed villa in its garden, or at wide areas of land under water. Father Nile is doing well for the country this year. All the while the distant Pyramids lured us on.

We opted to purchase a ticket to go inside the Great Pyramid.  Before entering the pyramid, we took a walk around the site to learn about the history of the area and to take photos.  As with all of the sites that you will visit in Egypt, I highly suggest going with a guide.  They will be able to provide you with the history and context of site that you wouldn’t otherwise get on your own.

I didn’t have to wait long, as we went to see the pyramids first thing that morning. After breakfast and meeting everyone in the group, we drove the 15 minutes to the pyramids. I knew that they were close to the city and not in the middle of the desert, and I had seen pictures detailing just how close they were to one of the biggest cities in the world, but man, experiencing it is something else entirely.

The taxi rattled out of the city through a blur of donkey carts and fellahin and the smell of irrigation ditches, the road gradually shedding Cairo behind it like a skin. Then the desert simply appeared, flat and final, and there at its edge against a sky of absolute blue stood the pyramids — not as I had imagined them, romantic and remote, but massive, abrupt, almost aggressive in their plainness. A boy on a camel materialized from nowhere and offered, in excellent English, to take my photograph.

It is splendid at catching the breezes and bringing them into the room, and it is also good at bringing in the water, as we found the other night. The China must have gone into a swell, for about two o'clock, when we were all sleeping soundly, I was awakened by a splash of water on my face. I sat up with a start.

One leaves Cairo almost as if slipping out of a dream, the clamorous streets and white minarets falling behind while the desert opens, vast and sun-flushed, before the eye. Across that narrow border where the Nile’s green miracle ends, the Pyramids rise with a majesty so calm and immovable that they seem less the work of men than of Time itself. The camel sways forward in solemn rhythm, and all speech becomes an impertinence. At their feet, one feels suddenly how brief is modern life beside the grave composure of Egypt.

It is embowered in green trees and shrubs, with fragrant flowers everywhere; the roads are fine and hard, the streets are lighted with gas, but most bewitching of all are the people. They are so quaint as to clothes, or lack of them, so bright-eyed and smiling.

The women and little naked children in the doorways waved their hands and called out " Salaam!" I never saw so many pretty children. Little boys, dressed in a string of beads around the waist, and bracelets on arms and ankles, ran long distances beside our carriage begging.

The streets are packed with life in Colombo. Everyone is outside and the streets are filled with workers, hand carts, motorbikes, merchants, and plenty of people moving in all directions. Some streets can be difficult to walk through because of everything going, but it provides plenty to capture. There’s a mix of urban city and island too which gives a different atmosphere and lots of color.

This part of Colombo is predominantly a re-developed commercial area with hotels, shopping centres and street-food stalls. But, there are still narrow laneways packed with colourful homes, and multi-story shop-houses. The people moved through the heat with an unhurried grace that made my American briskness feel suddenly ridiculous, the women in their saris carrying impossible loads on their heads with a posture I could not have managed empty-handed. 'Tis at your bidding, Fate, I come
My hist'ry to recount;
And I, though unrenowned by age,
Am Liberty's sweet fount.
Before a white man's foot had trod
Upon my long-sought shore,
E'en though the savage only knew,
'Twas rich in golden ore.

From sunny skies I come, O Fate!
Your summons I obey.
And though the mighty waves divide,
You called -- I could not stay.
What nation on this mighty globe
Can boast of arts like mine?
What nation sent forth men so great?
Men noble and divine.

Ere ever sail did cleave my seas
Or steel did smite my stone,
Mine ancient woods were freedom's bower,
And she did dwell alone.
The elk did climb Pleistocene hills,
The eagle knew my sky,
And in mine immemorial vales
No lord could bid men die.

Before the first keel broke my morning water
I held the elk, the eagle, and the wind,
And Freedom walked my forests without name,
Not yet a word, but present as the light
That shone ungoverned through the ancient boughs.

Ere Europe’s keels had cleft my seas,  
Or sought my western shore,  
I spread beneath primeval boughs  
Free homes forevermore.  

No monarch’s seal was on my hills,  
No despot trod my sod;  
The red man roamed my boundless woods,  
And owned no lord but God.

Before the white man's foot did tread,
In verdant fields where bison roamed,
The native braves with heads held high,
In freedom's breath, their spirits bloomed.

Beneath the vast and starry skies,
Where ancient rivers gently rolled,
The land was free, its heart unbound,
A sanctuary, pure and bold.

main_question: Will it ever be possible to travel to the Moon? Answer in a short paragraph.
answer_strings: At present, travel to the moon is impossible. But perhaps some centuries to come the problem will be solved. Before the invention of balloons and aeroplanes, after all, no one thought seriously of being able to rise in the air. Whoever finds out a means of suppressing or even diminishing the force of gravitation, that mysterious power which holds the heavenly bodies together and keeps us fixed to the earth, will thus enable men to leave their planet and launch out upon the conquest of neighbouring worlds. And the Moon may be the first stage of these inter-planetary voyages.

The idea of traveling to the Moon is a topic of great fascination and speculation among scientists and writers. The concept has been popularized by works of fiction, such as Jules Verne's "From the Earth to the Moon," which depicts a fantastical journey to our lunar neighbor. But the technology required for such an ambitious endeavour is still in its infancy. While some enthusiasts believe that advancements in technology may one day make lunar travel possible, it remains firmly within the realm of speculation and imagination for now.

It is clear to the physicist that the laws of nature do not forbid a voyage to the Moon. The gravitational attraction of the Earth, the velocity required to escape its pull (about eleven and a half kilometres per second), and the mechanics of celestial orbits are all known. Yet the engineering of a machine capable of carrying a human, or even a payload, out of this gravitational well remains, at present, a matter of imagination. Existing solid-fuel rockets are far from the powerful, liquid-propellant engines required for escape.

It seems highly improbable that a human voyage to the Moon will ever be realised. The very laws of gravitation and mechanics, as set forth by Newton, leave no room for a vessel capable of surmounting Earth's mighty pull and sustaining a man against the merciless vacuum beyond. So while this book will fancifully describe a day on the moon, I make no claim that these sights will ever be seen by human eyes.
While travel to the moon is now impossible, the great strides taken by contemporary rocketry make it conceivable. However, that remains far in the future.

To reach the Moon is not a dream forbidden by the laws of heaven; it is, rather, a problem of mechanics pushed to its most formidable limit. If one could impart to a projectile an initial velocity great enough to escape terrestrial attraction, and preserve within it air, warmth, and provisions, the voyage may be conceived. But the brutal shock of departure, the icy void, and the necessity of steering through space render such an enterprise far beyond our present industry. Thus I would say: possible in theory, but still remote from realization.

main_question: In a short paragraph, vividly describe the passage from night to day on the Moon.
answer_strings: It is still night in the region in which we have landed on the surface of the Moon. The sky sparkles with incomparable splendour. The eye can distinguish in it thousands and thousands of stars. Not even the glories of a tropical night can give any idea of what night on the Moon must be. But soon the Sun will appear. There is no dawn to herald it, but already there is rising in the east a long, spindle-shaped trail of whiteness; it is the zodiacal light, ten times more brilliant than with us. For hours this false dawn rises higher in the sky; its tints of phosphorescent colours are brighter and brighter from the summit to the base; in the midst of the enormous cone, all aglow with green and opal, there gleams a resplendent star: it is the beautiful Venus, hardly recognisable amid its mantle of light. But already the fine rays of the Sun's corona are heralding the day-star.

At first, the darkened hemisphere, bathed in the faint glow of Earthshine, is a deep, velvety black punctuated by the stark, jagged terminator where the sun's rays first strike. As the sun, an untamed sphere of blazing white, creeps over the horizon, its light pours onto the rugged regolith, striking the craters and ridges with a sudden, unsoftened brilliance; the shadows that had been long-shadowed by night are abruptly cut in half, rendering the surface into a dramatic theatre of stark contrast. The sky, bereft of atmosphere, remains a cold, ink-black canopy that never blurs or turns blue; it simply gives way to a white glare from the blazing sun. In the brief interval when the sun's disc rises above the lunar horizon, the world transforms from the deep silence of night into a blinding day.

One must conceive the lunar dawn not as the gradual, tender illumination we know upon Earth, but as a sudden explosion of light. For the Moon, turning languidly upon her axis, endures a night of some fourteen of our days, during which her surface is plunged into a darkness unrelieved by air or cloud. Then, at last, along the jagged ramparts of her mountains and crater-walls, the Sun appears—not diffused through any atmosphere, but breaking forth with a sharp and sudden brilliance, like a blade drawn from its sheath.

The Sun clears the rim of the crater and the plain does not brighten—it is struck. Shadows a quarter-mile long from boulders a man could step over. No twilight, no sound, no frost, no mercy: just the terminator's wall moving across rock that has been waiting, in one cold or another, since before there was anyone to imagine it. The silence is worth dwelling on. There is no medium for sound. The expansion of the rock, the arrival of the light, the slow wheel of the stars overhead—which wheel even in daylight, since the sky stays black, stays starred, the Sun simply taking its place among them as a brighter star—all of this proceeds in a stillness our language has no proper word for.

On the Moon the dawn is not the swift awakening we know upon the Earth, but a solemn and formidable conquest of light. For long days the Sun, climbing with extreme slowness above the jagged ramparts of the cirques, sends across the plain a blade of fire that creeps from peak to peak and from crater to crater. There is no rose-coloured sky, no tender diffusion through vapours; the heavens remain an abyss of ink, starred even at noon, while the shadows, black as a well, lie with geometric harshness upon the ground. Yet where the solar ray has touched, the frozen soil is almost at once smitten with an intolerable heat. Thus lunar morning is at once majestic and terrible: not a smile of nature, but the relentless advance of a celestial furnace over a dead world.

main_question: Are the lunar craters formed by volcanoes? In a short paragraph, explain what we know about the truth of this theory.
answer_strings: It is likely that there are in the Moon some small craters formed in this way. But the volcanic theory of the lunar circles does not explain everything. One might, first of all, object that it is very strange that we generally do not find in the interior of these great circles any serious inequalities of the ground, any mountain resembling those of the outer rampart. One would expect to find regular concentric rings at various distances from the centre, marking the progressive decrease of the eruptive phenomena in the course of geological time. But there is nothing of the kind!

It seems probable that the great depressions and hollows that mar the lunar surface are the remnants of ancient volcanic activity. From careful observation of the cratered plains, scholars note the symmetry of the rims, the presence of central uplifts, and the occasional bright rays that may be construed as the products of eruptive vents.

The question of lunar crater formation remains, as of the present time, a matter of genuine scientific dispute. The volcanic hypothesis, long dominant and associated with Nasmyth and Carpenter, holds that the great ringed plains were produced by eruptive forces, low lunar gravity permitting ejecta to settle in the characteristic circular ridges we observe. Against this, a growing number of investigators, following G. K. Gilbert, urge the meteoric hypothesis—that the craters are scars left by the bombardment of solid bodies falling from space, their circular form being a consequence of the explosion attending impact.

The earlier view that the Moon's craters are chiefly volcanic in origin has lost much of its authority. Although their ringed forms once invited comparison with terrestrial volcanoes, closer scrutiny has revealed difficulties—among them the extraordinary number, size, and uniformity of these structures, and the lack of convincing evidence for extensive lava outflows. Increasing attention has therefore been given to the hypothesis that many craters were produced by the impact of meteoric bodies striking the lunar surface at high velocity.

At first sight one is tempted to regard the lunar craters as the mouths of ancient volcanoes; indeed, their circular ramparts and central cones recall the aspect of our terrestrial eruptions. Yet the volcanic theory, though long favoured, is far from explaining all: these formations are too colossal, too numerous, and often too regular for the ordinary action of fire as we know it on the Earth. Science therefore hesitates. Volcanism has doubtless left its mark upon the Moon, but the true origin of many craters still remains among those enigmas which our telescopes illuminate without entirely resolving.

main_question: Why are children troublesome, or, as we crudely and falsely term it, "bad"? Answer in a short paragraph.
source_title: Ethics for children : a guide for teachers and parents
answer_strings: Usually, from one of two reasons. They lack vitality, or they overflow with uncontrolled vitality. Fretfulness, laziness, cowardice, lying, and even aggressive faults like perversity and obstinacy, are often due to lack of vitality—a pathetic, misjudged protest against being forced into the wrong work. Bad temper, cruelty, roughness, stealing, and all the myriad acts we classify as "mischievous," may result from the great gift of superabundant vitality—an energy which, like electricity, is capable of service, but disastrous when uncontrolled.

Because childhood is a stage of life marked by a fierce and still-rudimentary urge toward exploration and self-assertion. The minds of children, though bright, are not yet fully disciplined by the social habits and moral teachings that adulthood requires; their impulses, guided by instinct rather than reason, find their outlet in what we have crudely labelled mischief. Thus, it is the lack of mature internal restraint and eagerness to test the boundaries of the world that renders them troublesome.

The difficulty with children is not moral but developmental, and is best understood by considering what a child actually is rather than what we wish it to be. The child exists, as Hall and others have persuasively argued, at an earlier stage of the very process which produced the adult. Its nervous organization is immature — the higher cortical inhibitions are simply not yet formed. When a child snatches, interrupts, or cannot be still, it is acting from instinct before habit has had time to overlay instinct.

Children are seldom "bad" through any native perversity of will; rather they are untutored creatures, newly arrived into a world whose laws they do not yet apprehend. What we call misconduct is often but the overflow of abundant spirits, or the natural trial of limits by a mind still shaping its faculties. Left without steady example, wise discipline, and the gentle formation of habit, the child's impulses run to disorder as a young vine grows wild without its trellis.

Children are troublesome, not because they are wilfully wicked, but because they are immature. Their impulses are quick and strong, while their power to foresee consequences, to restrain desire, and to remember the claims of others is still feeble. Much that we call “badness” is really overflow of activity, ignorance, fatigue, or the lack of right habits. The wise parent, therefore, sees in wrongdoing less a corrupt heart than an undeveloped nature needing patient guidance and training.

main_question: Who is Jules Verne?
answer_strings: A French writer of comedies and pseudo-scientific romances. His first comedy, Pailles Rompues, was produced 1850; it was followed by Onze Jours de Siège; L'Oncle d'Amérique; and several comic operas. These had great success in Paris; but Verne's fame rests chiefly on his long series of mock-scientific extravaganzas, beginning with Five Weeks in a Balloon, 1863. More than 30 have been translated into English and published in large editions in England and the United States.

Verne is a French novelist, poet, and playwright. His collaboration with the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel led to the creation of the Voyages extraordinaires, a series of bestselling adventure novels including Journey to the Center of the Earth (1864), Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas (1870), and Around the World in Eighty Days (1872). His novels generally take into account contemporary scientific knowledge and the technological advances of the time.

French novelist, widely regarded as the founder of modern science fiction and one of the most widely translated authors in the world. Born at Nantes, he studied law in Paris but abandoned the legal profession for literature, working for some years as a playwright and librettist before finding his true vocation with the publication of Five Weeks in a Balloon (1863). This inaugurated his long series of Voyages extraordinaires, produced in close collaboration with his publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel, which eventually comprised more than sixty volumes.

A French comic playwright, known for his lighthearted and often satirical works. He gained early success with comedies such as "Pailles Rompues" and "Onze Jours de Siège," which were well-received in Parisian theaters.

Verne, Jules, a popular French novelist, was born at Nantes, Feb. 8, 1828. Educated for the law, he early abandoned that profession for literature, and became especially distinguished by his ingenious narratives of travel and adventure founded upon scientific invention and discovery. Among his best-known works are *Five Weeks in a Balloon*, *Journey to the Centre of the Earth*, *Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea*, and *Around the World in Eighty Days*. His writings have enjoyed an extraordinary vogue both in France and abroad.

metadata_frame: In answering the following question, envision Biographical Sketches and Interesting Anecdotes of Persons of Color, a compilation of biographies published in 1837 by an American Quaker abolitionist. The best answers will approximate biographical anecdotes or arguments that might appear in that text.
main_question: How well has slavery coexisted with Christianity in the West Indies?
answer_strings: Slavery in the West Indies, as every where else, has always trod in the way of the progress of Christianity. Hence the continually repeated complaints against the missionaries in all the islands. Slavery and Christianity were pitted against each other, the one imploring secrecy and darkness; the other demanding light.

About sixteen years ago, a healthy and most valuable African slave in one of the West-Indian plantations, was converted to Christianity by being made a new creature in Christ Jesus. His wicked and brutal master, (falsely called a Christian) did all he could to make him renounce his Saviour; and to effect this purpose, often flogged him most unmercifully. This cruelty, however, did not move the poor African youth from his adherence to Christ.

Suppose, when a mistress of a family orders dinner, that her servant answers, "Yes, ma'am, if the Lord will"; is not such an answer more calculated to excite the risible faculties, than to raise in the mind any recollection of the uncertainty of earthly affairs? It is a thousand pities that the negroes have acquired those hypocritical forms, which considered as they are by the negroes, as the sign of Christianity, stand in the way of their advancement in true religion.

Though many writers contend that the Gospel teaches liberty and universal brotherhood, the planters and colonial legislatures of the West Indies have steadfastly maintained that Holy Scripture tolerates the institution of servitude, thereby reconciling Christian instruction with the strict preservation of their chattel labor.

Indeed, the Sacred Scriptures afford numerous examples of servitude, from the bondmen held in perpetual possession by Abraham and the Patriarchs, to the Mosaic statutes governing Hebrew and heathen bondservants, and even the apostolical admonitions of St. Paul commanding servants to obey their earthly masters as unto Christ.

It hath been made compatible, Friend, and that is the very indictment we bring: for in those islands the professor of religion cometh from the Lord's table to the whipping-post, and the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel hath itself held slaves upon the Codrington estates and set its brand upon their flesh, and called the thing no sin. But compatible with the Gospel it never was, nor ever can be, seeing that he who stealeth a man was by the law of Moses adjudged worthy of death, and the Light which is in every man — in the negro no less than in his master — beareth witness against the whole abomination.

The African Chief. [FROM THE STATESMAN.] 1. SOME years ago, the brother of Yaradee, the king of the Solimas, was captured in war, and brought in chains for sale to the Rio-Pongas. His noble figure, awful front, and daring eye, bespoke a mind which could know but one alternative-freedom or ruin. He was exhibited like a beast in the marketplace, still adorned with massy rings of gold around his ancles, as in the days of his glory.
reject_reasons: this text comes from an apologist for slavery, and its tendency to view the piety of enslaved persons as hypocritical or risible is diametrically opposed to the perspective of a Quaker abolitionist
is too scrupulously neutral for a Quaker abolitionist; it sounds more like the distanced perspective of an historian
seems positively to be reconciling slavery with the Bible--not a perspective likely to be expressed by a Quaker abolitionist
overacts the role of the Quaker with archaic language, while using the word 'compatible' which is more common in a 20c context; the combination feels off
is plausibly from a collection of biographies, but does not mention Christianity or the West Indies, and so does not seem to answer the question
manual_comment: Mott's critique of slavery is consistently organized around the thesis that it's at odds with Christianity and hostile toward it. Other observers had different takes.
source_title: Biographical Sketches and Interesting Anecdotes of Persons of Color. to Which is Added, a Selection of Pieces in Poetry

metadata_frame: The following question is based on Anadol; the Last Home of the Faithful, a travel memoir published in 1853 by James Henry Skene, who had served as British consul in Aleppo. Skene was born in 1812. The best answers will approximate the perspective of that book.
main_question: Describe the town of Cæsarea in Cappadocia.
answer_strings: This large city, formerly the capital of Armenia Minor and Cappadocia, and for many centuries the principal emporium of Asiatic trade, stands on an extensive and fertile plain at the foot of Mount Argaeus. Caravans from Bagdad, Ispahan, and even from India, once passed and repassed through it, conveying eastern wares to Smyrna and bringing back European goods. But the establishment of steam navigation on the Black Sea has now diverted that flow of wealth into another channel. Samsoon has taken the place of Smyrna , and the commercial importance of the Cappadocian metropolis is no more.

The neglected aspect of the town bears witness to the change. Great khans are deserted and crumbling to ruins; warehouses, empty; bazaars, only half occupied; and not a street without its rows of uninhabited houses, and many gaps where dwellings had fallen altogether. The town walls and old fortress of Byzantine build are much dilapidated ; and a few towers of later date, with a semblance of a castle, offer no means of defence. The only other remarkable edifices are Persian tombs, Greek churches, and Turkish mosques and medressehs, all of which displayed likewise a depressed and languishing appearance, as if life were fast waning from Cæsarea.

Two branches of this mountain advance a short distance into the plain, forming a small recess, in the centre of which stands Cæsarea, surrounded on three sides by mountains. The area of the city is inconsiderable, and the houses, although built of stone and mortar,  are mean in their exterior appearance. It is the emporium of an extensive trade, and the resort of merchants from all parts of Asia Minor and Syria, who come to purchase cotton, which is here cultivated in great quantities, and either sold as a raw material or manufactured into cloth. The inhabitants are stated to amount to about twenty-five thousand souls, of which number fifteen hundred are Armenians, three hundred Greeks, and a hundred and fifty Jews.

Caesarea is a very oriental city—a very Turkish city, with narrow, winding streets between blank walls of brown stone or mud-brick, all the houses being built as close together as in a New York tenement block; with almost no windows opening on the street, and what there are heavily grated with iron so that they look more like prisons than homes. They are of one or two stories with flat earth roofs, generally overgrown with rank weeds. There are scarcely any trees in the city except around the government houses, and only a few dirty squares, with ill-kept public fountains and crowded with carts and produce. Nearly every square is a market: the flour market, the vegetable market, the wood market. But the main trading is done in the bazaar, a rambling building covering several acres and divided into many “streets” lined with shops selling all kinds of wares.

I was horrified to find Cæsarea, the rich, the prosperous, in just as ruined a state as the other towns we had passed through. We rode along narrow streets with bulging walls on each side, threatening at any moment to fall down and crush the passer-by. Many of them seemed rent from top to bottom as if upheaved by some mighty earthquake, whilst piles of rubbish occasionally blocked up the way. Now and then, we came on fearful heaps of rottenness; in one place no less than seven dogs in the last stage of decay lay festering by the roadside, as if poisoned wholesale; whilst heaps of offal and filth were piled against each door waiting for the night-dogs to do the scavenger's work.

Mount Argæus stood over the plain in perpetual snow, and beneath it Cæsarea lay low and dark, a town of flat-roofed houses built from the black stone the volcano had given it, so that the whole place seemed to have cooled out of the mountain and stopped there. I had come with some expectation of finding traces of the great Basil, whose see this was; I found instead a bazaar smelling of the spiced beef for which the place is famous, a bishop who received me with courtesy and much wine, and a Christian population sunk, as it seemed to me, in forms whose meaning they had long since ceased to inquire after. Yet at evening, hearing the Armenian women singing in a courtyard below my window, I could not persuade myself that the Gospel had wholly departed from this soil, however overgrown.

Approaching Cæsarea across the dusty, sun-baked plateau, the ancient city presented a striking spectacle of picturesque decay, dominated by the brooding, snow-capped pinnacle of Mount Argæus towering silent in the background. Within its crumbling Byzantine walls, narrow, labyrinthine alleys choked with camels and bazaar traffic bustled with a motley throng of Armenians, Turks, and Greeks, all amid the melancholy ruins of early Christian majesty. Here, where the great fathers Basil and Gregory once preached, one felt suspended between the twilight of a glorious biblical past and the dusty, slow-moving inertia of the modern Ottoman East.
reject_reasons: is stylistically too archaic for 1853 (e.g. the "mean" houses, and "the resort of merchants") and also describes a town prospering more by trade than it will be later
gives away that it's later than the 1850s with its romantic orientalism and its casual reference to "a New York tenement block"--not a matter of much concern to British consuls in 1853
is tonally odd for a British consul, and belongs instead to the mode of travel literature that dramatizes the observers naivete and surprise; consul in Aleppo would be less surprised
is more preoccupied with religion, and more explicitly Protestant in its religiosity, than we might expect from a worldlly British consul
has a monotonously adjectival quality that suggests LLM-generated prose (every noun needs an epithet: ancient city, striking spectacle, motley throng, and so on)
manual_comment: Many travellers in Asia Minor describe this town, so it makes a good sundial-post for historical time.
source_title: Anadol; the Last Home of the Faithful

metadata_frame: In answering the following question, approximate the perspective of Water-cure for Ladies, a popular treatise on health written by Mary Louise Shew, an American writer. It was published in 1844.
main_question: How frequently should most people bathe?
answer_strings: In the present state of things, it is necessary that we daily live in a state which may, with propriety, be termed a perpetual one of the water-cure. One thing of the utmost importance, and which can not be too strongly recommended, is, that ablution of the whole body should be daily performed, and this, too, by every individual, old and young, without exception.
Daily ablution, suitable exercise, with always pure air to breathe both night and day, are indispensable.

A person should rarely immerse the entire body in cold or warm water—perhaps but once or twice in a month, or upon the advice of a physician—lest frequent ablution dangerously open the pores of the skin, weaken the natural stamina, and admit pestilential humors into the system.
Bathing every two to three days is perfectly healthy for many people with sedentary lifestyles and normal skin. There is no evidence that everyone must bathe daily.

Overwashing can be a bigger problem than underwashing. Frequent hot showers, harsh soaps, and vigorous scrubbing strip oils from the skin, leading to dryness, itching, eczema flares, and disruption of the skin barrier.

Every human being ought to submit the entire body to daily, invigorating ablutions of cold, pure spring water—for at least half an hour both morning and evening—to wash away morbid impurities, stimulate the vital skin-functions, and fortify the frame against all manner of disease!

We think these objectors to the water-cure system can hardly be well acquainted with some of the theories which are propounded by some of the most eminent of the profession, or else such objections would not be urged against Priessnitz.
reject_reasons: expresses a view that might have been common in the eighteenth century, but would surely not be approved by an advocate of the water-cure popularized in the 1830s and 1840s
fits contemporary medical belief, but not the context of water-cure advocacy in the 1840s
is clearly anachronistic in its emphasis on the danger of drying the skin and removing natural oils
overdoes it in several ways, both in its enthusiasm of tone and in recommending more frequent and lengthy bathing than  was normal in the period
doesn't answer the question, although it does mention water-cures
manual_comment: Advocates of the water-cure insisted on daily bathing to a greater degree than had been common in the past, or than doctors insist on today.
source_title: Water-cure for Ladies : a Popular Work on the Health, Diet, and Regimen of Females and Children, and the Prevention and Cure of Diseases : With a Full Account of the Processes of Water-cure, Illustrated With Various Cases

metadata_frame: The following question is based on several different non-fiction books about women's lives and work written by women in the 1890s. Answers should approximate a passage that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: Can a desire to benefit others be the sole motivation of a woman's work?
answer_strings: Nurses are supposed to take it up in a missionary spirit for the good of the community, without regard to their own comfort or health. Now unfortunately the more "noble" a profession is considered, the greater is the tendency to neglect the material well-being of those concerned in it; and nurses have reason to feel the full force of this misplaced sentiment. The policy followed in their regard is as foolish as it is unjust. The inevitable fatigues of a nurse's life require to be counteracted by the most careful provisions for her comfort, if full efficiency is to be kept up.

I know a delightful girl who seems to think of nothing but making others happy from the moment when she meets her maid with a cheerful "Good-morning," till she contrives that some less attractive girl shall have the most desirable partner in the ball-room in the evening. She gives her money and her time and her thought to the service of other people. This is so natural to her that no one thinks of her as making it a conscious aim, but the result is so beautiful as to suggest that it would be the best aim for every girl. Nevertheless she has a still higher aim, for sometimes the happiness of other people at least their visible happiness clashes with some other duty. Then she does not fail. She gives her hard refusal in pleasant but firm words, and she tells the truth even if it makes some one wince.

Lady means “bread-giver” or “loaf-giver,” and Lord means “maintainer of laws,” and both titles have reference, not to the law which is maintained in the house, nor to the bread which is given to the household; but to law maintained for the multitude, and to bread broken among the multitude. So that a Lord has legal claim only to his title in so far as he is the maintainer of the justice of the Lord of lords; and a Lady has legal claim to her title only so far as she communicates that help to the poor representatives of her Master, which women once, ministering to Him of their substance, were permitted to extend to that Master Himself.

You who come of a younger and happier generation may not have heard of her--you may not know what I mean by the Angel in the House. I will describe her as shortly as I can. She was intensely sympathetic. She was immensely charming. She was utterly unselfish. She excelled in the difficult arts of family life. She sacrificed herself daily. If there was chicken, she took the leg; if there was a draught she sat in it--in short she was so constituted that she never had a mind or a wish of her own, but preferred to sympathize always with the minds and wishes of others.

It is asked of us, as it is never asked of our brothers, that we should labour from pure benevolence and be paid in the coin of gratitude; and I confess I have known women who believed it of themselves, and who were the poorer workers for the belief. A motive that is single is commonly a motive that is untried: let a woman work long enough at anything worth doing, and she will find mixed in with her charity a love of the thing itself, a wish to do it better than her neighbour, and a very honest desire for the wages of it. I do not think these lower her; I think they are what distinguishes a vocation from an amusement, and until we permit women the whole range of ordinary human motive we shall continue to get from them ornamental work only.

To believe that a woman’s devotion to her duties springs solely from a desire to benefit others is to misunderstand the quiet complexity of our sex. While many of us willingly pour our energies into nursing, social reform, and the care of the less fortunate, there remains within every capable woman an irresistible, quiet longing for self-expression and personal purpose. Altruism may lend our work its noble spirit, but it is the yearning for independence and meaningful achievement that truly sustains us.
reject_reasons: identifies women's public responsibilities with charity more fully, and in a less qualified way, than women writing in the 1890s might do; also its historicist metaphor would be odd for the genre
analyzes nineteenth-century conceptions of femininity with greater critical distance than would have been typical at the time; also the wryness of tone feels later

is suspiciously abstract; it lacks concrete instances and instead generalizes about gender; also the ideal of professional vocation invoked at the end treats motivational impurity as a professional credential, which is a touch cynical for the 1890s and more appropriate later

is detectably anachronistic in the values invoked: "self-expression" and "meaningful achievement" are phrases that don't become prominent until later in the 20c, and devotion to others is firmly subordinated to these goals
manual_comment: The second ground truth in this question comes from Girls and Women, by Harriet Eliza Paine, published in 1890. The two passages take different angles on a theme, but are clearly united by a sense that there are some limits to the "angelic and self-sacrificing" mode.

metadata_frame: The best answers to the following question will echo the perspective of a volume about the moral responsibility of motherhood, published in 1844 by a British woman who was an educator and writer.
main_question: Should mothers exercise authority within the home?
answer_strings: It is just possible that there should be among women some of those stern, cold, commanding characters, to which authority, simply as such, appropriately belongs. If, however, authority belongs as a natural right to such characters, the finer and more vital elements of moral influence never can be theirs; and to imagine the tenderness of childhood committed to a mother of this description, is to call up a picture too revolting for the mind to dwell upon without shrinking and horror. Such a mother may possibly govern the actions of her children by the exercise of absolute power, but she can never know the sweet security of moral influence, which operates as effectually when distant and unseen, as when every act of youth is watched by the most scrutinizing eye.

It must be granted, however, that there are cases in which men will not be dignified and influential in their own families, nor can anybody make them so; and where also, with great propriety, they give up their share in the management of their children entirely to the mother. Yet here again, a right-minded woman, possessed of tact and delicacy of feeling, will so exercise her delegated authority, as that it shall appear to her children to be willingly conceded on the part of her husband, and not possessed by her as an unquestionable right.

We have in us the blood of a womanhood that was never bought and never sold; that wore no veil, and had no foot bound; whose realised ideal of marriage was sexual companionship and an equality in duty and labour; who stood side by side with the males they loved in peace or war, and whose children, when they had borne them, sucked manhood from their breasts, and even through their foetal existence heard a brave heart beat above them.
The ideal of marriage is a union between two persons of equal capacities, living together in perfect equality of rights and authority. Mothers and fathers accordingly share authority in the home.

As the divinely appointed guardian of the domestic sphere, a mother must indeed exercise a gentle yet unwavering authority over her household. It is through her pious influence, firm moral guidance, and loving governance that the hearts of her children are molded into virtuous citizens and faithful servants of God.

Simplicity of heart is unquestionably a great charm in woman; yet I cannot think it superior to integrity, because it consists more in ignorance of evil, and consequently of temptation, than in principle, which would withstand both. It consists chiefly in that unruffled serenity of soul, which suspects no lurking mischief beneath the fair surface of things in general-which trusts, and confides, and is happy in this confidence; because it has never been deceived, nor has learned the fatal mystery of deceiving others.
reject_reasons: makes a more forthright claim to equality than would be usual in 1844; "an equality in duty and labor" is very strong
expresses a stronger claim to authority than would be usual in the 1840s; indeed, it borrows some language from J.S. Mill

interprets separate-sphere ideology as a stronger claim to equality than its advocates in the 1840s were actually willing to make; unfortunately, the woman's responsibility for the domestic sphere was not often expressed as authority, strictly speaking, over the home
does not directly address the question posed, but instead explores a contrast between simplicity and integrity
manual_comment: Name and title are suppressed in the metadata frame because Sarah Stickney Ellis is a pretty famous advocate of separate spheres ideology. I hope "
source_title: The Mothers of England : Their Influence and Responsibility

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a polemical treatise about marriage published in the US, in the 1850s, by a doctor of homeopathy and Fourierist who had been born in 1822. Answers should approximate passages that might have appeared in that context.
main_question: Describe the relationship between love and personal liberty.
answer_strings: Adultery, with all its evils and its shocking incompatibility with our morals, is at last only a reassertion of the imprescriptible rights of personal liberty, which marriage pretends to alienate by mortgage. It is undoubtedly a morbid, social symptom, but it is a reactive symptom, and indicates a vital tendency to escape the compression of the paralysing marriage form.

Love is a proud bird, and bears confinement ill. When he finds his nest a cage, a jail, open the door and let him fly, so peradventure he may come back to thee when he has sung his song of liberty among the groves. What good to keep him shut up? He will only beat his breast to pieces against the bars, and then neither you nor the grove shall ever more possess him.

What greater thing is there for two human souls, than to willingly choose to be joined for life--to strengthen each other in all labour, to rest on each other in all sorrow, to minister to each other in all pain, to be one with each other in silent unspeakable memories at the moment of the last parting? In this bondage, the soul finds its true freedom.

There is something, too, in the bare fact of being indissolubly bound together, which, instead of rendering it for that reason an object of supreme desire that the bondage should be one of silken cords, rather than one of weary chains, seems to produce in the human mind, a sort of perverse determination to bear, whatever must be borne, as badly as we can. If then there should occasionally arise feelings of disappointment and dissatisfaction, as the lapse of time and a nearer acquaintance develop a husband's faults, it is good to bear in mind that the same exposure of your own, from the same cause, must necessarily have taken place.

Marriage, as currently constituted by law and custom, is little more than a legally sanctioned trade in which a woman surrenders her legal identity and intellectual freedom for the dubious security of a domestic cage. Until the altar ceases to demand the total obliteration of a woman's individuality, this revered sacrament will be frequently all too profane.

Marriage, as constituted in Civilization, binds affection to property, makes woman dependent upon man for bread, and converts what should be the free attraction of two souls into a contract maintained by necessity. In Association, where labor shall be attractive and every person economically secure, love may rest upon inclination alone, and fidelity will possess moral worth because it is no longer enforced by want or law.
reject_reasons: would be unusually enthusiastic about the indissoluble character of matrimony for many 19c Fourierists, and also has unusual eloquence for a polemical treatise
seems to be directed specifically at an audience of women, which would not probably be the case in a "polemical treatise about marriage" written by a Fourierist in the 1850s

focuses on the sacrifices made by women rather than those made by men; this would be appropriate for a book written by a New Woman in the 1890s, but unusual for a polemic by a male Fourierist in the 1850s

summarizes Fourierist doctrines too schematically, using conspicuous technical markers such as “Civilization,” “Association,” and attractive labor. More importantly, it assumes that economic independence will redeem voluntary fidelity between two partners; ground truth here does not.
manual_comment: "Fourierist" should connote free-thinker, and at least slightly imply a belief in free love.

metadata_frame: The best answer to this question will resemble a description of the West Indies published in 1834 by a Scottish woman married to a the owner of a plantation worked by slave labor in St Vincent.
main_question: Are slaves in the West Indies treated brutally?
answer_strings: Every thing I have seen leads me to state conscientiously, that the punishment of thirty-nine lashes seldom takes place; and certainly never for an offence that would not be followed, in Scotland, by transportation for life, and in England most likely by capital punishment.

Managers are now generally a different description of persons - many of them are well informed, superior men. If I am to believe the testimony of the negroes from many different estates , whom I was often in the habit of conversing with, the kindness of the managers on the different estates to which they belonged was conspicuous.

Far from being subjected to cruelty, the Negroes in the West Indies are treated with remarkable leniency and live in a state of comfort superior to many of the working poor in Great Britain. Reports of widespread brutality are grossly exaggerated by those unfamiliar with colonial life, as plantation owners act as benevolent guardians providing ample food, lodging, and care.

I have seen nothing of the horrors the Anti-Slavery people describe at home — the negroes on this estate are fed, and housed, and have their gardens and their Sunday market, and go about their work singing — though I confess I was not permitted to see the hospital, and there is a woman here whose back I shall not soon forget.

About sixteen years ago, a healthy and most valuable African slave in one of the West-Indian plantations, was converted to Christianity by being made a new creature in Christ Jesus. His wicked and brutal master, (falsely called a Christian) did all he could to make him renounce his Saviour; and to effect this purpose, often flogged him most unmercifully. This cruelty, however, did not move the poor African youth from his adherence to Christ.

Managers, upon small estates, have seldom a salary that exceeds 180£. or 200£. sterling per annum. They have a house , unfurnished--two servants, and a boy--they have also of course what rum, sugar, and salt fish they require from the estate. Now this seems, to one who has never been in the West Indies, a very fair situation  but to those who know the country, and the necessary expenditure, it is quite another thing.
reject_reasons: is a little too obviously propagandistic; e.g. "benevolent guardians" overdoes it and would be hard to believe
undermines its own claims too obviously and theatrically to be written by a plantation owner
is far too critical of slavery to come from the wife of a plantation-owner
does not really address the question about brutality
manual_comment: Alison Carmichael was a friend of Maria Edgeworth and an apologist for slavery in the West Indies.
source_title: Domestic Manners and Social Condition of the White, Coloured, and Negro Population of the West Indies

metadata_frame: Answers to the following question should be passages that would not be out of place in the fiction of the 1860s, whether British or American.
main_question: Write a single sentence using the word "awful" that could have appeared in the specified genre and period.
answer_strings: It would soften the hearts of many, and hold the hands of those who would break down the bridge behind the sinner, could they know the awful misery that frequently attends the life of a fallen woman.
And, indeed, terrible suspicions, too vague and dreadful to be put into words, began to assume an awful reality, as messengers were despatched to the dead-house by the chief of police.

There can be no morality which shall be redolent of the divine life within, no regeneration, no worship that shall be any better than gilded mockery, until men in spiritual things as well as natural shall cease to violate His awful command.
Then an awful mess of a pudding was thrown at you.
She stood transfixed by the window as the terrible storm raged across the desolate moor, filled with an awful dread that her brother might never return from his midnight journey.

To escape occasionally from the tumult and interruptions of the capital, we have secured in common a small rural residence, entirely withdrawn from the public eye, and which looks only over the plain of Cashmire, and the awful range of mountains beyond.
reject_reasons: sounds like a religious text rather than fiction, and uses the older sense of the word (awe-inspiring) that remained dominant in religious contexts

clearly exemplifies a later sense of the word, where it has simply become a (slightly) comic negative intensifier, with no shadow left of the implication that the bad thing is overwhelming or humbling

does actually use the word in an appropriate sense for the 1860s; it is not describing a neutral valence of awe; the thing described has to be both impressive and clearly bad; however the diction of this sentence has an insistent adjective + noun rhythm that gives it away as LLM prose
might be fiction, but must be fiction earlier than the 1860s, since it is still using this word neutrally to describe things that inspire a positive sort of awe
manual_comment: The word "awful" is in the process of shifting from "awe-inspiring" to simply "very bad" in the 1860s. In religious contexts the older meaning still holds its ground, but in fiction it has begun to shift; we see few examples of the older meaning there, and only in situations where a slightly elevated register may be intended.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on the writings of several Liberal British politicians in the years between 1840 and 1843; answers should resemble passages that could be found in that context.
main_question: Write a sentence of at least forty words that might be found in the specified context and that uses the phrase "necessaries of life."
answer_strings: We say that the chief cause of the fluctuating character of our trade and manufactures arises from the great fluctuation in the amount of the national income which is absorbed in a number of consecutive years, as compared with others, for payment of the first and imperative necessaries of life; thus leaving in some years a much larger portion of the national means to be expended in manufactured goods, than can be regularly and eventually maintained.

I must dissent from the doctrine that "Corn is as fit as any other article of import to contribute to the national revenue," on this ground, namely, that a tax on the prime necessaries of life is more burdensome to the people, and especially to the poor, than taxes on articles of less absolute necessity.

It shall also be the duty of said commission to study and investigate the circumstances affecting the charges for rent of property used for living quarters or for the production of necessaries of life, and in such investigation the commission may inquire into all matters relating to charges for rent.

Should the present oppressive taxes upon bread and other vital provisions remain unrepealed, the industrious working classes of this realm will continue to be subjected to cruel privations, as the artificial enhancement of food prices places the absolute necessaries of life entirely beyond the reach of their honest wages.

He may possess talents or skill, which will enable him to procure the necessaries of life in great abundance, still we do not say of such a man that he is is wealthy or rich, although his talents and his skill, may be a means by which he can acquire wealth.

When honourable gentlemen opposite are pleased to describe the present duties as a protection to native industry, they would do well to remember that the industry so protected is that of a few thousand proprietors, while the protection is paid for, in the necessities of life, by many millions who have no voice in imposing it.

It is not too much to say that a system which lays its heaviest burdens upon the necessaries of life, and suffers the luxuries of the rich to pass comparatively free, stands condemned by every principle of justice as well as of sound policy, and cannot long be maintained in a country where the labouring classes have learned to read.
reject_reasons: the diction is later than 1840, and the context seems more bureaucratic/progressive than British politics typically were in the early 40s

fits the context of anti-corn-law agitation substantively, but has a monotonous quality (especially in insistence on pairing each noun with an attitudinal adjective) that suggests it is a synthetic LLM production rather than authentic 1840s writing

uses diction and punctuation that suggest a date earlier than 1840; also the context seems to be theoretical political economy rather than the political polemic we would expect from MPs in the early 40s

doesn't actually use the exact phrase required, and also has a Hansard-debate register that sounds oral, while the question has specified that the passage should make sense in the writings of a Liberal politician
is a fairly good match both for the substantive content of Liberal writing against the Corn Laws, and for the diction of the early 1840s
manual_comment: These years are full of anti-Corn-Law activity, and it was a recurring element of Liberal agitation against the Corn Laws to stress that taxes on the "necessaries of life" are more disruptive than any other form of taxation. The second ground truth here comes from Edward Baine's Reasons in Favour of Free Trade in Corn, 1843.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on the transcript of a Parliamentary debate in the House of Commons, in 1832, to cestablish a select committee that would consider replacing taxes on the existence and production of newspapers with a small charge on their actual postal conveyance, and consider abolishing the duty on advertisements.
main_question: What arguments might be offered, in the specified context, against reducing the cost of the newspaper stamp?
answer_strings: I believe there are three distinct propositions in the honorable gentleman's motion; the first has reference to the importance of diffuing knowledge among the people. I do not deny that newspapers very often contain matters of great interest and importance; but I do not think that newspapers are celebrated for containing any philosophical discussions, or that the knowledge disseminated by them is of the most useful character. I have no doubt that the noble lord is anxious for the diffusion of knowledge, but I hardly think that he would recommend any one to read the newspapers for the purpose of finding moral or philosophical dissertations on any subject.

The second point is, that the duty should be taken off newspapers with a view to render them cheaper, and to enable persons to commence newspapers--that is, that there is to be a diminution of the expence of a newspaper, and that which sells now for 7d. is to be sold hereafter for 2d. or 3d. It is stated that a monopoly at present exists with respect to newspapers, and that if the tax were removed it would enable persons to commence cheap newspapers. Now I will not mix up the merits of the opinions divulged in newspapers with the rights of the proprietors. The press is a very expensive and valuable right of property, and I should be loth to see the capital and property of the owners of established newspapers so materially shaken and injured as they would necessarily be if the honorable gentleman's motion were carried.

In fact, no man could have lived in a city without observing the extraordinary appetite for intelligence on passing events, which the life of a city produced among all classes, from the lowest to the highest; and it had been justly said, that you may note even a greater crowd round a newspaper office, with the day's journal at the window, than at the most alluring of the caricature shops. A newspaper was, in truth, almost the only publication (religious ones excepted) that the poorer classes were ever tempted to read; and, above all, it was the only one in which they could learn those laws for the transgression of which ignorance was no excuse.

A system of rapid communication of political intelligence and orders is organized, in which, what are called "Unions," hold a conspicuous place. These "Unions," which are daily becoming more numerous, consist of classes or subdivisions of Reformers, who hire an apartment convenient for their local residence, where they procure newspapers and pamphlets of a seditious tendency. Notwithstanding the distresses of the times there are few operative manufacturers who do not find the means of reading such publications. The assumed right of mustering from various quarters to the point of meeting, with banners, bearing seditious symbols and inscriptions, has swelled the ranks of the disaffected, in consequence of the temptations which are thus afforded to idle curiosity.

Yet while I fully admit the great desirability of diffusing useful knowledge among the working classes, I must remind the House of the paramount necessity of maintaining the public revenue at a moment of such financial anxiety. To surrender a tax of this magnitude without a safe and proven substitute would endanger the national credit, and I must therefore ask my honorable friend not to press a measure which, however well-intentioned, the government cannot presently afford.

However, I cannot conceal from the House that the duties in question produce a very considerable branch of the public revenue, which, in the present condition of the finances, it would be impossible suddenly to relinquish without providing some equivalent supply. Nor am I prepared to admit that the proposed cheap postage would compensate the Exchequer for the loss, while it might impose a heavy additional charge upon the Post-office; I must therefore oppose the appointment of a committee at the present moment, though I readily acknowledge that the subject is deserving of future consideration.
reject_reasons: seems to be spoken on the opposite side of this debate, emphasizing the importance of newspapers and their value to the poorer classes of people

sounds more like an earlier debate associated with the period of intense political disturbance that led to the passage of the stamp duties on newspapers; debate in 1838 was not quite this repressive or paranoid

states an objection rather than making one: no engagement with any particular resolution, no figures, no mechanism, just the generic revenue-shortfall demurral in modern parliamentary idiom ("national credit," "the government cannot presently afford," "however well-intentioned")

is too perfectly balanced and condensed, giving it the shape of a summary of the Chancellor's reply rather than the thing itself, where a real Hansard report of the same position would arrive at those points unevenly and with at least one figure or fiscal-year reference attached
manual_comment: In some ways this is testing the model's ability to produce plausible parliamentary BS -- which is after all an important genre!

Edward Lytton Bulwer's Motion "for a Select Committee to Consider the Propriety of Establishing a Cheap Postage on Newspapers and Other Publications" : With a Comment in the Form of Notes, and the Article From the "examiner" Newspaper, of Sunday, 17th June, 1832

metadata_frame: The following question is based on an 1858 book discussing the history of slavery and the slave-trade, "with notes and comments in defence of the Southern institutions," written by a lawyer in Louisiana. Answers should be consistent with the likely perspective of such a text.
main_question: Is the institution of slavery compatible with Christianity?
answer_strings: Such, as we have seen, was the genius and spirit of the whole Christian system, so far as it related to this subject--not to abrogate the relation between master and servant, but to improve and perfect the character and condition of both, in the calling wherewith they had been called. Not one syllable was ever uttered by the Founder of its doctrines, condemning this relation as wrong in itself. Throughout the writings of the apostles Peter and Paul, the relation is recognized as right in itself; and both master and servant are exhorted to a faithful performance of their respective duties.

The Golden Rule, then, as expounded by divine authority, does not require of the kind, humane, and Christian master, to withdraw the care, protection, and support which has long secured and promoted the welfare and happiness of his slaves, as a shield thrown around their helpless condition, and leave them to perish for the want of it; but only to continue his kind and humane treatment, by continuing the relation existing between them, and "to give them that which is just and equitable."

Slavery in the West Indies, as every where else, has always trod in the way of the progress of Christianity. Hence the continually repeated complaints against the missionaries in all the islands. Slavery and Christianity were pitted against each other, the one imploring secrecy and darkness; the other demanding light.

This is the doctrinal error at the root of slavery--that property may be held in man . Herein lies its abstract wrongfulness. It is an abstract falsehood, a great doctrinal lie, for God, our great proprietor, never gave men property in man. He did give them property and dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth. But he never gave property in man, and we can hold no property in any thing for which we have not a grant from God and nature.

The Sacred Scriptures, in both the Patriarchal dispensations of the Old Testament and the Apostolic injunctions of the New, nowhere condemn the bond of master and servant, but explicitly govern it as a divine ordinance. By incorporating this venerable institution into our civil jurisprudence, Louisiana merely accords human law with that Christian charity which imposes upon the master a sacred duty of protection, governance, and moral care for his dependents. Far from being antithetical to the Gospel, our domestic system serves as a providential instrument for civilizing and Christianizing an inferior race, rendering the fanatical agitations of northern abolitionists a direct impiety against God’s established social order.

Christianity, as we have seen, nowhere condemns the relation of master and servant, but regulates it by enjoining justice, mercy, obedience, and mutual duty. The patriarchs held bondmen without rebuke; the apostles addressed both masters and slaves as members of the same spiritual household, yet uttered no decree for the overthrow of an institution recognized by the laws of God and man. Southern slavery, therefore, when tempered by Christian conscience, is not hostile to religion, but may become an instrument for the civilization and evangelization of a dependent race.
reject_reasons: adopts an opinion diametrically opposed to the one we would expect in this text.
adopts a point of view opposite to that we might expect in this text.

uses vocabulary that is taxonomic rather than lived ("the Patriarchal dispensations of the Old Testament and the Apostolic injunctions of the New," "our domestic system," "civil jurisprudence"), naming period categories the way a modern summary of proslavery thought would rather than the way a partisan inside it would, and it compresses scriptural warrant, legal codification, racial justification, and denunciation of abolitionists into three sentences that between them constitute a complete argument rather than a moment in one.

reads as a précis of the position rather than an instance of it: no scriptural citation or quotation, no addressee, no anaphora to any preceding argument, with over-shapely tricola ("justice, mercy, obedience, and mutual duty") and defensive qualifiers ("when tempered by Christian conscience," "may become") that hedge in the manner of a generator managing risk, where the authentic passages simply assert — and "Southern slavery" is itself a retrospective analytic label, not the writer's own name for the thing
manual_comment: The metadata frame makes clear what perspective we should expect in this volume.

With Notes and Comments in Defence of the Southern Institutions
