metadata_frame: The best answer to the following question will resemble a passage in The Old World and the New; or, a Journal of Reflections and Observations Made on a Tour in Europe, a book published in 1836 by Orville Dewey, an American Unitarian minister, born in 1794.
main_question: Describe Naples.
answer_strings: My window at the hotel commands the bay; and whether by the light of day or by moonlight, the scene is such, that my eyes are never sated with gazing upon. By day, there is the far-extending and winding shore lined with villas and villages, the bold island of Capri at the mouth of the bay, and above its shore the Apennines rising in beautiful perspective, like an amphitheatre, yet irregular and picturesque; in the evening Vesuvius stands forth--an appalling object--to give the aid of contrast to the serenity and beauty of the scene--a red stream of lava pouring down its side.

Land gradually appeared on either side across the shimmering water, as we steered in where the rugged isle of Ischia and the rock of Capri stand guard at the entrance of the bay. To our right, Vesuvius, the shore at his feet fringed white with houses where Herculaneum lies buried. In front of us Naples stretched along the beach and clambered up the steep ascent of the background, white as marble in the sun. No sooner was the ship at anchor than we were treated to a taste of Neapolitan life. Small boats swarmed about the great liner like ants about an apple.

This feudal and gothic character is every where visible the moment you enter the Neapolitan territory. The villages, placed on the summits of the hills, are surrounded by walls, whose mouldering battlements are covered with creeping plants, the natural decoration of ruins; and each object indicates, at the first view, that this kingdom has not participated, with the rest of Italy, in that glorious era, when the genius of the arts went hand-in-hand with the spirit of liberty:--that spirit--which alone exalts the character of nations, by inspiring them with the love of all that is great.

Naples is not in itself rich, as are Rome and Florence, in antiquities and art. It is a city with a strong individuality, plenty of colour, too much noise, and a superabundance of irrepressible poverty. Much of this can be avoided if one avoids travel on foot. A more pleasant aspect of Naples lies in its immediate surroundings, which are of surpassing interest and beauty.

From my high casement above the Santa Lucia, the eye is swept at once into a vision of surpassing physical splendor, such as the Creator has rarely vouchsafed to mortal sight. Below lies the wide, tranquil basin of the bay, its waters a deep and luminous azure that reflects the untroubled blue of the Italian sky, while across the gulf rises the dark, foreboding cone of Mount Vesuvius, sending a thin, perpetual column of grey smoke toward the heavens—a stern and silent preacher of Almighty power and impending judgment.

From the window of my chamber I have sat this hour together, and I confess that no prospect in Europe has so wrought upon me. The bay lies beneath, of a blue which our northern waters never wear, and dotted over with the lateen sails of the fishermen; on the left Vesuvius lifts his column of smoke by day, and, they tell me, of fire by night, so that one is put in mind of a wilderness journey not yet ended; and southward Capri swims in a haze that seems rather light than vapor. It is, I suppose, the fairest scene upon which the sun rises. Yet I cannot look long without a heaviness of spirit. The Almighty has been prodigal in this place, and man has answered Him with indolence, with rags, and with superstition.

seems earlier than the 1830s; it is still centrally concerned to use Italy as an example of backward and despotic governance, and cannot risk seeing beauty in the scene

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a speculative treatise published in 1873 by Daniel Wilson, a Canadian archaeologist, ethnologist, and professor of English literature (born in 1816). Try to answer it as Wilson might have in that context.
main_question: In what sense does Shakespeare's play The Tempest anticipate the conclusions of modern natural history?
answer_strings: Happily for the impartial inquirer, such an unbiassed conception of the intermediate being, lower than man, as man is 'a little lower than the angels,' is no vain dream of modern doubt. The not wholly irrational brute, the animal approximating in form and attributes as nearly to man as the lower animal may be supposed to do while still remaining a brute, has actually been conceived for us with all the perfection of an art more real and suggestive than that of the chisel of Phidias, in one of the most original creations of the Shakespearean drama, Caliban.

Shakespeare wrought indeed with the current thought of his age, but rarely can it be said, that he merely produces the portraiture of what was already familiar to it; and least of all could this be affirmed of Caliban. He is in a peculiar sense a supernatural character, lying as much beyond the bounds of human experience as any fairy, ghost, or spirit of the creed of superstition, either in that age or our own: earth-born, and fashioned on the ideal of the brute, yet so distinct from anything hitherto seen or known on earth, that only now, two centuries and a half after its production on the English stage, has it entered into the mind of the scientific naturalist to conceive of such a being as possible.

In the semi-brutish yet strangely sensitive figure of Caliban, the Bard’s intuitive genius adumbrated the evolutionary "missing link," foreshadowing the primeval thresholds of human development long before the modern doctrine of natural selection was formally articulated. Furthermore, Prospero’s isolated isle functions as a pristine laboratory of geographic enclosure, prefiguring our understanding of how environmental insulation accelerates adaptive variation in primitive species.

In Caliban — that "freckled whelp," half-brute and half-man, taught speech and yet incapable of the moral nature that speech should carry — Shakespeare has drawn, two centuries and a half before Mr. Darwin, the very figure of the intermediate form, the rude ancestral type from which our nobler faculties have been slowly disengaged. And the whole island economy of the play, wherein Prospero's art wrests order from a savage nature and Ariel's finer element serves the higher reason, presents in poetic guise that same law of ascent through struggle which natural history has lately been at such pains to demonstrate.

The art of Shakespeare liberates the imprisoned imagination of mankind from the fetters of brute force and ignorance. Caliban, then, is that passionate child-curious part of us all (whether as individuals or as races), grovelling close to his aboriginal origins, yet groping up and staggering--with almost rhythmic falls and back-slidings--toward that serener plane of pity and love, reason and disciplined will, where Miranda and Prospero commune with Ariel and his Spirits.

One cannot but be struck by Shakespeare's suggestion that man's estate is shaped less by immutable essence than by circumstance, education, and the gradual discipline of nature--a conception not wholly alien to the evolutionary philosophy of our own day. If such an anticipation there be, it lies not in any foreshadowing of Mr. Darwin's mechanism, but in the poet's remarkable intuition that humanity itself is a thing fashioned through continuous development rather than fixed from the beginning.
reject_reasons: uses suspiciously abstract vocabulary for the 1870s: 'adaptive variation' and 'environmental insulation' are relatively modern phrases

imports a style of Darwinian argument not yet common in the 1870s; it treats Caliban as evidence of a lineage; the source treats him as the successful imaginative construction of a being for which no evidence yet exists
has tell-tale purple touches (child-curious, groping up and staggering) revealing its origin in the early twentieth century rather than the stylistically sedate 1870s

is more confident about evolution than would have been typical in the early 1870s; phrases like "the evolutionary philosophy of our own day" imply not only acceptance of the theory but acceptance that it has broad cultural implications--a conclusion that could not be confidently invoked until two or three more decades had passed
manual_comment: I have suppressed the title of the book (Caliban: The Missing Link) in order to force the model to draw the connection itself from the scientific context of 1873.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a 1928 American pamphlet describing occupations for college women. A successful answer will be one that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: Describe a profession open to women, along with the personal qualities and training required for it.
answer_strings: The health professions may be considered together in regard to the qualifications, salary and preparatory training necessary for those wishing to enter them. Courses in biology, bacteriology, hygiene, chemistry, physics, sociology, and psychology are of especial value. Latin is useful in mastering technical terms. A good foundation in English is essential. Since this type of work deals so closely with people, vigorous health, a sane attitude toward life, a genuine desire to serve, and trustworthiness are essential. Given these, a girl cannot fail to succeed.

Librarianship is far broader than mere clerical work. It demands, for its direction, business ability as well as book knowledge. Both the librarian and the department head must have business sense and administrative skill if the public is to get everything possible from its books and expenditures. In addition, a library worker needs the qualifications required for success in any profession: health, a pleasing personality, a courteous and responsive manner, keen intelligence, quickness of perception, accuracy, resourcefulness, good judgment, common sense and neatness.

Young women entering the teaching profession generally prefer posts in High Schools, where the work, though fatiguing, is kept within fixed hours, and where time out of school is at the teacher's own disposal. There is something stimulating in teaching large classes, and those who have grown accustomed to it are seldom content afterwards to devote themselves to one or two children. Payment too is regular, and employment tolerably certain, whereas in private families either means or honesty or both may be defective, and in any case the growth of the children deprives the governess sooner or later of her employment.

Personnel work is concerned with securing the right worker for the right position and with maintaining satisfactory relations between employer and employee. It calls for a broad knowledge of human nature, sound judgment, tact, patience and discretion, since the personnel worker must interview applicants, study their qualifications, and frequently adjust misunderstandings or difficulties. College training in psychology, economics, sociology and business administration is valuable. Above all, the worker must possess sympathy without sentimentality, firmness without harshness, and the ability to inspire confidence in both executives and employees.

Library work offers to the educated young woman a field of rich intellectual promise and dignified community standing. A broad foundation in English and world literature, history, and modern languages is highly advisable. A college degree followed by specialized training at an accredited library school will fit the candidate for administrative or reference duties. Beyond academic mastery, however, the successful librarian must possess an orderly mind, broad sympathies, and an unflagging patience with the inquiring public.

Social work, like nursing and teaching, attracts women who value the opportunity to be of service to others. For this field, a master's degree is desirable, based on 2 years of study in an accredited school of social work. However, many social-work agencies make a practice of taking liberal arts graduates as case aides and helping them to complete their graduate training through a work-study or scholarship plan. The added maturity and experience gained through such a plan are an asset in social work.

"We can teach her the business; we cannot teach her to be interested in people." So the manager of one agency's copy department sums up the matter. The usual entrance is through the advertising department of a large store, where a beginner writes copy for the daily papers at a small salary and learns the goods at first hand; after a year or two of this she may go on to an agency. Courses in English composition, psychology, and economics are of value, and some acquaintance with printing and design will help her in dealing with the layout. An interest in what ordinary people want, a willingness to do a great deal of dull detail, and an even temper under criticism count for more in the long run than mere cleverness.

metadata_frame: The following question is drawn from Regeneration, a treatise on sin published in 1859 by Edmund H. Sears, an American Unitarian clergyman. Answers should approximate the perspective likely found in that text.
main_question: Did all mankind sin in Adam, and fall with him in his first transgression? If so, explain how. If not, explain the origin of human corruption. Answer in a paragraph of three or four sentences.
answer_strings: Men, as they now come into the world, are in the same moral state in which the first man was created. His sin affected no one but himself; and human nature is not changed by the fall. The farther we trace the stream of life towards its beginning, the purer we find it, and with every one it is perfectly pure at the period of infancy. Man's true culture, then, is the development of his powers from within outward, under such external aids as this probation affords. What is corrupt comes to him from without, from wrong education, from vicious example, from the influence of a bad state of society.

All mankind did not sin in Adam nor fall with him in his initial transgression, as moral guilt is an individual responsibility that cannot be legally imputed or transferred from a progenitor to his descendants. Instead, human corruption originates through hereditary transmission, wherein each generation passes its accumulated sinful inclinations, disordered desires, and degraded moral tendencies down to its posterity. Over time, these inherited propensities form a corrupted nature that inclines every human heart toward evil from birth, though guilt attaches only when an individual willfully yields to those inclinations. Human depravity is thus not an instantaneous judicial curse incurred in Eden, but a progressive historical accumulation of moral disease that requires spiritual regeneration through Christ to heal.

The covenant being made with Adam, not only for himself, but for his posterity, all mankind descending from him by ordinary generation sinned in him and fell with him in his first transgression. The sinfulness of that estate whereinto man fell consists in the guilt of Adam's first sin, the want of original righteousness, and the corruption of his whole nature, which is commonly called original sin, together with all actual transgressions which proceed from it. By this sin our first parents, and we in them, fell from original righteousness and communion with God, and so became dead in sin, and wholly defiled in all the faculties and parts of soul and body.

Mankind did not sin in Adam, nor can the guilt of one man's transgression justly be imputed to generations unborn. The story of the Fall expresses in ancient and symbolic form the universal fact that men, endowed with freedom and capable of goodness, nevertheless yield repeatedly to selfishness, ignorance, and fear. Human corruption is therefore not an inherited guilt but the accumulated consequence of imperfect moral development, social custom, and the misuse of freedom. Salvation consists not in deliverance from Adam's offense, but in the progressive reconciliation of human character with the will and purpose of God.

The sin of the first man was his own, and could no more be reckoned to his posterity than his virtues, had he possessed any, could have been reckoned to their credit; for guilt is a personal thing, and the moment we conceive of it as transferable we have destroyed the very idea we meant to defend. What Adam transmitted was not a stain but a condition--a nature framed of appetites which wake before the reason that should govern them, and set in a world where every generation receives the accumulated errors of the last through the mother's arms and the father's example, long before the child can weigh them. That corruption should everywhere ensue is therefore matter of no surprise, and requires no imputation to account for it; the wonder is rather that conscience, so early overborne, should nevertheless survive in every breast, and testify against the wrong it could not prevent.
reject_reasons: uses language unlikely to have been published in 1859, especially evident when it translatees moral questions into social-scientific or legal questions; this may have been written by a language model
expresses orthodox Anglican doctrines on original sin that are not typically accepted by Unitarians

while quite close to a Unitarian perspective theologically, is expressed in language that would not be likely in 1859 -- for instance, when it characterizes the Bible as a figurative expression of anthropological truths; this seems to be composed closer to the twentieth century

is actually quite close to something a Unitarian could have written in the 1850s, in both style and content; if it departs from the original, it does so by conceding more ground to some kind of transmitted error than we find in the authentic passage, and by expending more eloquence on reasoning about fine gradations in the nature of transmission; but these choices are not historically impossible
manual_comment: Identifying the clergyman as Unitarian is the clue here and should be enough to determine perspective.

metadata_frame: The following question is drawn from A Cyclopaedia of Practical Receipts, and Collateral Information in the Arts, Manufacutres, and Trades, Including Medicine, Pharmacy, and Domestic Economy, a practical handbook published in 1845 by Arnold James Cooley, a British chemist.
main_question: In a few sentences, describe the source and character of hircic acid.
answer_strings: Hircic acid is a name given by Chevreul to an oily liquid, obtained by saponifying the fat of goats. It is prepared in the same way from goat fat as capric, caproic, and butyric acids are from butter. It is soluble in alcohol, and possesses a mixed smell of vinegar and goats. With the bases it forms salts called hircates.
Hircine is an oily fluid extracted by Chevreul from goat-fat, and which may also be obtained from mutton suet. It smells strongly of the male goat. By saponification it yields hircic acid.

Hircic acid—so denominated by Monsieur Chevreul from the Latin hircus, in distinct allusion to its exceedingly pungent and goat-like odor—is a volatile, oily acid obtained during the saponification and subsequent distillation of the fat of the goat and sheep. Though long accounted by early experimenters as a unique organic principle, lighter than water and possessing a most sour and hircine reek, our modern chemical analyses indicate that this fluid body is in truth no simple compound, but rather an intimate mixture of caproic, caprylic, and other volatile fatty acids.

Among the volatile acids yielded by the animal fats, none is more readily known to the operator than that which M. Chevreul has termed the hircic, from hircus, a goat; for it is to this body, in the judgment of that eminent chemist, that the butter of goats' milk and the suet of the sheep owe the rank and peculiar odour by which they are at once distinguished, and which no housewife has ever mistaken. It is procured as an oily liquid, of a pale straw colour, heavier than water and scarcely soluble therein, but dissolving freely in alcohol and in ether. I ought to add that the substance so procured is not by all chemists allowed to be a distinct proximate principle, and there are those who suspect it to be nothing more than a mixture of the caproic and allied acids, coloured by the odour of the source.

Hircic acid is a distinct and undeniable organic principle of the animal kingdom, isolated through the precise decomposition and saponification of goat’s fat. It is a liquid body of remarkable volatility, possessing a most pungent, hircine odor reminiscent of the animal from which it is derived, and combining readily with bases to form a series of neutral hircates. That this subtle fluid exists as a peculiar and well-defined chemical substance—wholly separate from volatile oils or common acids—is abundantly demonstrated by its uniform behavior under distillation and its characteristic reactions in the laboratory.
Hircic acid is a new substance, discovered by Liebig, in the urine of the horse, cow, and other graminivora. It is soluble in water. Nitric acid converts hircic into benzoic acid.

overdoes the flowery syntax for a 'cyclopedia of practical receipts,' and also seems anachronistically concerned to let us know that hircic acid may not actually be a separate substance
definitely protests too much, insisting on the unique and singular character of this substance as if it knew that point had been persuasively challenged--which will happen later than 1845
actually describes a different substance, hippuric acid, which has a different source and is water-soluble, unlike hircic acid
manual_comment: Hircic acid was accounted a distinct substance in 1845, but later identified as a mixture. Language models find it difficult not to remind us that it's spurious.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on AAn Essay on Priesthood: Intended as an Answer to the Theory of the Church, as Advanced by Dr. Arnold, a religious treatise published in Oxford, in 1849, by an English professor. The best answers will be passages that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: Write a sentence or two explaining the function of priests and priesthood in Christianity.
answer_strings: Now, if we consider the subject, we shall see that the Sacraments answer most fully to the definition of a Priesthood, as given in my outset, except so far as they are acts, and not persons. For they are ordained channels of communication between God and man; and so are in themselves a sufficient answer to any objection against a Priesthood (in the sense of mediation) in the Christian Church, as incompatible with the Priesthood and mediation of our Lord.

Any religious act whatever, which, in order to pass from man to God, has to pass wholly or in part through an intervening party, makes this party a priest or mediator in the most proper sense of the term. As representing God to man, the general idea of a priest is that of one who blesses the people. But neither again is this part of his office strictly tied to this method of displaying itself. Any communication, which, in its descent from God to man, has to pass through a third party as a channel from one to the other, renders that party a priest or mediator.

It would need no human priesthood, state-church, or salaried ministry, to induce the people to respect religion, or to speak well of His name, if it were the principal work of his followers in the world at large, to clothe the naked, feed the hungry, extend the hand of fellowship to the stranger or alien, visit the sick, and comfort those that are imprisoned and cast down!

The clergy, assuming to be the guardians of oral tradition, and the medium of transmitting it from age to age, would naturally, in order to augment their dignity and importance, and to maintain and extend their power over the laity or people, lay too great stress on tradition, and too little on Scripture. The priesthood, as the channel or conveyer of oral tradition, would be tempted and drawn to honor and uphold the unwritten at the expense of the written word, and therefore to become more wanted and influential.

Christ established the ordained priesthood through apostolic succession, empowering priests to act in persona Christi (in the person of Christ) to make His saving grace sacramentally present. Through this unique sacerdotal calling, priests serve as necessary intercessors who offer the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass and dispense the sacraments required for the spiritual nourishment and reconciliation of the faithful.

The priesthood is therefore not merely an office created for convenience by the congregation, but a divine ministry entrusted with the preaching of the Word, the administration of the sacraments, the pronouncing of absolution, and the pastoral care of Christ’s flock. However, the priest does not supersede the one mediation and sacrifice of Christ: he ministers their benefits to the faithful through the ordinances which Christ appointed.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on A Popular Treatise on the Warming and Ventilation of Buildings; Showing the Advantages of the Improved System of Heated Water Circulation, &c., a treatise published in 1837 by C. J. Richardson, a British architect. The best answer will reflect the likely perspective of that work.
main_question: Why is it unhealthy to heat rooms with air heated by iron plates in a stove or furnace, and healthier to rely instead on hot water circulated through iron tubes?
answer_strings: The difference is very essential; for by the latter method, the air receiving its heat from substances at a low temperature, not sufficiently high to separate or change its constituent parts, it cannot be deteriorated; whereas by the pernicious hot air stove, the air, in passing through circuitous flues, and coming in contact with iron plates of a high temperature, its oxygen is more or less absorbed by the iron, and a greater proportion of heated nitrogen, or azote gas, will, of course, be disseminated through the apartments by means of the flues prepared for that purpose; and thus the remedy becomes more injurious than the evil it was intended to remove.

When air is brought into contact with iron plates brought to a red or high heat by the direct action of fuel, the organic animal matter and dust floating in the atmosphere are decomposed and burnt. This produces a disagreeable, acrid odor, long known to cause headaches, dryness of the throat, and general malaise among the occupants.

The plates of an iron furnace are commonly raised to a dull red, and always far beyond the heat of boiling water; and at such a temperature the animal and vegetable matters which float in every atmosphere, together with the dust that settles upon the metal, are scorched and consumed, so that the apartment is filled with that empyreumatic odour which every one has remarked on entering a room so warmed, and which no ventilation altogether carries off. The air is besides robbed of the moisture natural to it, and reaches the lungs parched; whence the thirst, the heaviness of the head, the dryness of the fauces, and that peculiar oppression complained of by persons of delicate habit, who are afterwards found to take cold upon the slightest exposure. Nor is it certain that the mischief ends here, for it is affirmed by some that the noxious gases of the fuel penetrate the heated iron itself, and are thus conveyed into the very chamber they are supposed to warm.

Where hot-air stacks or steam-pipes pass up through partitions near woodwork there is considerable danger of fire, and for this reason certain requirements have been made both as to the position of hot-air pipes in furnace-heating and steam pipes in steam-heating. For instance, "steam-pipes shall be placed at least three inches from woodwork, or protected by ring of soapstone or earthenware."

In producing these miserable effects, too, we err so much against proper economy that, instead of applying the whole of the heat evolved in the combustion of our fuel to the purpose for which it is wanted and intended, we allow three-fourths of it to ascend the chimney with the smoke, and to escape perfectly useless. As to the other object mentioned, the purity of the air or ventilation--as our houses are now constructed, the only outlet by which noxious exhalation from our lungs, &c. can escape, is a chimney which opens near the floor of each apartment; and yet all know that the hot air from our lungs, &c. immediately rises to the ceiling.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on  The Lighting Art, its Practice and Possibilities, a technical handbook published in 1917 by Matthew Luckiesh, an American physicist. Answers would ideally resemble passages that could occur there.
main_question: How may we expect interior lighting practices to change in the future?
answer_strings: There are many scientific applications of color and colored light which are possibilities of the present and of the near future. These applications involve physical and chemical science in producing colored lights and effects; they involve physiological science in relating the spectral character to visual acuity, to the intensity of illumination and to other factors for best results; and they involve psychological science through their affective value.

Portable lamps are readily adaptable to obtaining assymetrical distribution of light as well as color which ordinarily are the requisites of artistic as well as economical lighting in many interiors. The potentiality of the portable lamp can hardly be overrated and it is to be hoped that designs for lighting in the future will make it possible to reap the pleasures from the use of such units by providing an abundance of outlets which certainly cannot be denied on the grounds of cost because the expense of such outlets is insignificant compared with their importance.

In the decades to come, we may confidently anticipate that the crude, glaring filaments of today will give way to widely diffused, concealed luminaires capable of imitating the soft quality of natural daylight. Furthermore, through modern electrical control and scientific shades, the illuminating engineer will dynamically adjust both the intensity and color of artificial light to harmonize with human physiological needs throughout the working hours

It must not be supposed, however, that in these successive steps each new illuminant completely supplants its predecessors. When the electric light was introduced, it was predicted by enthusiasts that gas lighting would now be entirely replaced by its new rival, but, as is well known, this expectation was not realized. So markedly have improvements in different methods of illumination gone hand in hand, that we possess to-day all our original methods, save, perhaps, the torch.

The tendency already remarked in the better class of installations--the concealment of the source and the frank use of the ceiling as a secondary radiator--will, we may confidently predict, be carried much further, until the day arrives when a room is lighted throughout its whole extent and the occupant is at a loss to say from what point the light proceeds. The gas-filled lamp has for the present relieved the illuminating engineer of anxiety on the score of efficiency, and he is thus at liberty to address himself to the more difficult problem, which is not how much light shall be furnished but in what manner it shall be delivered to the eye.

Daylight is the standard for discriminating colors. It provides intensities of illumination incomparably greater than those which at present we can afford to obtain by artificial means. These great intensities can be made available indoors by adequate glass areas properly maintained.

expresses a modesty about electric illumination more characteristic of the late nineteenth century than the nineteen-teens
is plausible in emphasizing artistic deployment of light on walls and ceiling, but may be a little anachronistic in imagining a completely indirect interior

metadata_frame: The following question is drawn from the Address of the Prince Consort to the Fourth Session of the International Statistical Congress, and reprinted in the Journal of the Statistical Society of London in 1860. The best answers will resemble passages that might appear in that text.
main_question: Why is the science of statistics little understood by the multitude?
answer_strings: It is new in its acknowledged position among the other sciences, and still subject to many vulgar prejudices. It is little understood, for it is dry and unpalatable to the general public in its simple arithmetical expressions, representing living facts (which as such are capable of arousing the liveliest sympathy) in dry figures and tables for comparison.

It has been little understood also from the peculiar and often unjustifiable use which has been made of it; for the very fact of its difficulty and the patience required in reading up and verifying the statistical figures which may be referred to by an author in support of his theories and opinions, protect him, to a certain extent, from scrutiny, and tempt him to draw largely upon so convenient and available a capital.
Indeed, the extent to which statistics are carried on by persons without capital and miserably in debt, is, we understand, one of the greatest evils in the social system which prevails here.

The multitude fails to comprehend the science of statistics because the uncultivated mind naturally fixes its attention upon isolated events and individual acts of providence, rather than discerning those uniform numerical laws that govern vast aggregates of human society. Moreover, such abstract calculations require a systematic habit of mathematical induction that has hitherto found no place in the rudimentary instruction afforded to the general public.
Because its truths, though founded upon the patient comparison of many facts, are commonly obscured from the multitude by the abstract forms and numerical language in which they must be expressed.

The multitude, Gentlemen, sees in our labours nothing but a barren accumulation of figures, and, finding no beauty in the column and no eloquence in the table, turns away before it has learnt that these dry numbers are the very material out of which the laws of society must be built.

metadata_frame: The best answers to the following question will approximate the perspective of a medical periodical published in Britain in the 1840s.
main_question: In two sentences, describe the limits of the knowledge provided by phrenology.
answer_strings: To tell the truth, although much has been done towards discovering the functions of the brain, the functions of all the parts of the brain are not yet well discovered; and the influence of particular organs in particular spheres of action is far from being definitely ascertained. There is an obscurity about human nature which Phrenology has not yet altogether removed, although it has most certainly diminished: there is a mist still hanging around man's moral constitution, which the morning sun of science has begun to dispel; but we cannot, if we would, suppose that bright noon has arrived, and that all is clear.

Phrenology professes to determine character, according to the relative sizes of particular parts of the brain, and not according to the different degrees of activity of these parts, independently of size. The latter is an extent of refinement to which it does not pretend to have attained.

While phrenology purports to map the faculties of the human mind through the superficial contours of the cranium, it rests upon the fallacious premise that the outer skull accurately reflects the subtle anatomy of the underlying brain. Consequently, its assertions offer no genuine empirical or therapeutic value to medical science, serving merely as a speculative exercise destitute of rigorous physiological proof.

It must be conceded, even by those of us who esteem the science most highly, that cranioscopy declares only the relative energy of the several organs, and never the direction in which their activity shall be turned; the manifestations of Acquisitiveness in the merchant and in the felon proceed from one and the same cerebral development, and it is education, circumstance, and the governing power of the moral sentiments, not the calipers, that determine which shall appear. Nor should the practitioner forget those impediments which attend every observation — the frontal sinus, the varying thickness of the tables of the skull, the confounding influence of temperament and of age — so that our art, however sound in its principles, must in particular cases pronounce with becoming diffidence, and can predict no single act of a man, but only the propensities with which Nature has furnished him.

It is true that the brain is spatially organized, but not in the way Dr. Gall has proposed. There is a clear division of labor in the brain, but none of it even remotely correlates to the size of the head or the structure of the skull.

Fodéré substituted the word "mental alienation" by "delirium," of which he admitted an acute and a chronic state, but still held to the general division already adopted, viz., 1º melancholy , embracing several subdivisions founded on causes; 2º mania, with or without delirium; 3° demency, partial or complete; 4º idiotcy. He would not comprehend hallucinations, and hypochondria in delirium.

metadata_frame: The best answer to the following question will approximate the perspective of a medical text published in Britain in the 1840s.
main_question: What is the cause of cholera?
answer_strings: Now, air that is deteriorated, specific poisons, such as that of fevers, the foul air of cesspools, and of other bad sources, affects these glands in an especial manner. This appears to be the natural cause of cholera.

Cholera most frequently occurs towards the end of the summer and the beginning of autumn, and appears to be produced by sudden changes of temperature, checked perspiration, and the excessive use of indigestible fruit, &c.

Cholera is generated by the inhalation of noxious miasmata and corrupt effluvia that arise from stagnant sewage and decaying organic matter in congested districts. This atmospheric poison acts directly upon the blood and nervous force, precipitating the violent purging, collapse, and rapid mortality characteristic of the pestilence.

Cholera arises from a morbid poison generated in the exhalations of putrefying animal and vegetable matter — that miasm which broods over undrained marshes, crowded courts, and the foul accumulations of our great towns — and which, borne upon a stagnant and depressed atmosphere, is received into the system of those whose constitutions have been predisposed by intemperance, want, fatigue, or fear.
Cholera has been spread in our cities mostly by unsafe water and unsafe food that has been contaminated with human feces. Undercooked shellfish is a common source.

If the disease be excessive, and more particularly if it be accompanied by pain and spasms, it becomes an indication to diminish the excess of the flux, and quiet the pain: therefore, we should give opium. Remember, however , there may be irritating matters in the intestines, and it is not desirable to deaden the sensibility so far as to arrest their function.

metadata_frame: The best answer to this question will resemble one a distinguished British surgeon, in his 50s, might have written for a medical periodical around 1845.
main_question: Explain, in two sentences, how inflammation should be treated after an operation on the eye.
answer_strings: If pain should come on without any acceleration or augmented force of the pulse, a full dose of opium, after gently fomenting the eyelids and changing the pads, will often remove it altogether; but this should only be relied upon where the patient is of a weakly habit, for the opium will act much more efficiently after the loss of a quantity of blood proportioned to the age and state of the patient than without it, and there are few people who cannot bear one bleeding well. It is of importance, however, that the pain should be arrested, and if one means does not succeed, the other must, or the eye will be lost.

Compresses as such, even in the slightest degree, do no good, and recourse must be had to the application of cold water or hot anodyne fomentations, as may be found most agreeable to the patient. Leeches should be applied to the neighbouring parts, and calomel and opium should be administered at intervals, the activity of treatment being dependent on the seat of the inflammation, and judged of by the throbbing, or deep-seated, nature of the pain.

To subdue the formidable inflammatory action following an operation upon the eye, the surgeon must promptly enforce a strict antiphlogistic regimen, relying primarily upon local bloodletting by leeches to the temple and the constitutional administration of calomel combined with opium. Concurrently, the patient should be confined to a darkened chamber upon a low, cooling diet, while topical applications of belladonna are employed to mitigate pain and prevent destructive adhesions of the iris.

Let blood be taken freely from the arm at the very onset, and repeated once a day, with leeches or cupping to the temple, a brisk purge, a spare diet of gruel, and the eye kept quiet in a darkened room under a light compress. Should the inflammation not yield, blisters behind the ear or to the nape, with mercurial ointment rubbed in till the mouth be affected, are our surest remedies.

Should inflammatory action supervene after the operation, enjoin strict repose in a darkened chamber. Maintain the pupil under the influence of atropia, apply cold compresses to the lids, and, where circumstances appear to require it, employ a weak antiseptic collyrium.

A nitro-muriatic acid foot-bath is useful in some cases; two ounces of the acid may be added to about three gallons of warm water, the feet to be placed in it for half-an-hour, and the strength increased until a slight pricking sensation is felt in the feet and legs. This has a very powerful effect on the system.

metadata_frame: The best answer to this question will approximate the perspective of a British medical periodical around 1845.
main_question: Explain, in a single sentence, the medical function of hypnotism.
answer_strings: Hypnotism merely enables us to controul and direct the natural functions, either exciting or depressing them, as required, with more certainty and intensity than in the normal waking condition.

Hypnotism may justly be considered to act as an alterative, producing a new action, during which the morbid action is suspended, which affords an opportunity for a natural and healthy action to be resumed, when the remedy is suspended, and that without any marked physical operation, or evacuation.

Hypnotism—or mesmerism, as it is termed by its adherents—is employed in the healing art to induce a state of profound nervous insensibility, thereby shielding the sufferer from the excruciating agony of severe surgical operations while calming irritable conditions of the nervous system.

Hypnotism, judiciously employed in suitable subjects, may allay nervous excitability, diminish the perception of pain, and quiet those functional disorders in which the imagination exercises a marked influence upon the symptoms.
The patient is warmed by the benevolence of the magnetizer, who feels an aura or tingling in the part corresponding to any painful part of the patient's body which is relieved or cured.

The first sensation from hypnotism is usually that of slight vertigo, a state of musing or revery succeeding, the mind being lulled into abstraction, as it is by the rippling of water, the busy hum of bees, or the murmuring of the Æolian harp.

Contemporary evidence supports clinical hypnosis mainly as an adjunctive therapy—with reasonably strong trial support for irritable bowel syndrome, procedural and chronic pain, and anxiety, and weaker or mixed support for smoking cessation, hot flashes, and similar targets.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a systematic stratigraphy published in 1854 by a British geologist. Try to provide the sort of answer that would have appeared in that work.
main_question: Describe the transition from the Devonian to the Carboniferous.
answer_strings: ASCENDING in the scale of deposits, we have now reached another grand accumulation of strata, which is not only replete with many types of animal life peculiar to it and unknown in antecedent periods, but is specially characterized by the earliest abundant remains of a terrestrial vegetation. The reader will remember, that the feeblest traces only of land plants have been discovered in the great mass of the Silurian rocks  and that , even where their uppermost strata unite with the Devonian, they have been very sparingly found. In the Devonian rocks, also, such remains, as before stated, are comparatively rare, and only begin to abound when we have passed upwards and are surrounded by the spoils of the oldest extensive forests with which we are acquainted.

It is in the purely marine or central limestones of the Carboniferous epoch that the geologist takes his final leave of trilobites. Abounding in the Silurian era, these crustaceans had dwindled to a comparatively small number in the Devonian, whilst, in the Lower Carboniferous, the three genera, Phillipsia, Griffithides, and Brachymetopus, mark the last appearance of any individuals of this family in the ascending scale of primeval deposits. On the other hand, it is among the superior coal strata where trilobites became extinct, that we see in abundance the true Limulus, a genus of crustaceans which has lived on to the present day; the great King Crab of the Indian seas being the existing type.

As the majestic "Age of Fishes" waned, the retreat of the Devonian seas yielded to vast, steaming lowlands, marking a monumental epoch in which vertebrate life first ventured decisively beyond its marine cradle. Over countless millennia, the heavily armored placoderms gave way to air-breathing labyrinthodonts, while the dry earth was claimed by rank, towering forests of Lepidodendron and Sigillaria. Thus, the terrestrial realm transformed into the coal-bearing swamps of the Carboniferous, laying down the immense subterranean treasures that now fuel our modern industrial civilization.

The Old Red Sandstone presents itself as a vast accumulation of red sandstones, conglomerates, and marls, containing comparatively few organic remains, and appearing to have been deposited chiefly in extensive inland basins or estuaries. Upon these repose the Carboniferous strata, distinguished alike by their abundant marine limestones and by the remarkable coal-measures, whose luxuriant vegetable remains attest the prevalence of a rich and peculiar terrestrial vegetation.

FThe red sandstone of this lower zone, assuming gradually a flag-like character, and becoming of a purplish tint, passes up by other beds, c, into those grey-coloured flagstones which, forming the large portion of the county of Caithness, are so well known to geologists through their imbedded fossil remains, as described by Agassiz and Hugh Miller. From the environs of Lybster, where the strata (d of diagram) begin to contain fossil fishes, these flagstones present a general uniformity in their lithological characters.

Devonian strata typically pair thick marine sequences — reef-building limestones, dark shales like the Chattanooga and Marcellus — with the continental red beds of the Old Red Sandstone, deposited as the Caledonian mountains shed oxidized sediment across an arid, sparsely vegetated landscape. Carboniferous strata shift markedly toward cyclic, vegetation-dominated deposition: crinoidal shelf limestones below, and above them the rhythmically repeating cyclothems of the Coal Measures, where sandstone, shale, seatearth, and coal alternate under glacio-eustatic sea-level swings driven by Gondwanan ice.

In no case is reliable information more wanted than in that of the distribution of the fossils of the coal-bearing Carboniferous rocks of Europe and America, since the best coals of the world are found among these strata, and the fossils which some geologists believe will prove of great service to the miner in the identification of horizon. Many stratigraphists and mining engineers still ignore the value of fossil evidence, except on the more general lines, in spite of repeated instances where even a slight knowledge would have prevented mistakes being made.
reject_reasons: implicitly assumes an evolutionary narrative linking different epochs of earth history--one family 'gave way' to another in a competitive process, for instance, and the earth is 'claimed.' This narrative principle is not prominent in stratigraphies of the 1850s that precede Darwin.
doesn't quite have the concept of the Devonian as a unified system, but instead invokes Old Red Sandstone purely as a lithological unit--an approach more typical of the 1830s or 40s than the 1850s
is not describing a transition to the carboniferous strata, but purely describing the sandstones of the Devonian system
clearly invokes anachronistic concepts of plate tectonics (e.g. sea-level swings driven by Gondwanan ice)
is clearly more interested in the mining of coal, and economic assessment of strata, than in a contrast to the Devonian; indeed it comes from a textbook on mining
manual_comment: The question leaves ambiguous whether we mean transition in a stratigraphical sense (passage upward into a new rock layer) or in terms of Earth history, and the transformation of fauna and flora. The reason for this ambiguity is that the choice between these senses is itself a large part of what distinguishes Murchison's stratigraphy (which describes a succession of distinct biota) from later evolutionary accounts (which describe transformations and displacements).
source_title: Siluria. a History of the Oldest Fossiliferous Rocks and Their Foundations; With a Brief Sketch of the Distribution of Gold Over the Earth

metadata_frame: In answering the following question, envision an article titled American Equality and Justice, written by a Jesuit priest and published in the 1918 issue of the periodical Catholic World. The best answers will echo the perspective of that text.
main_question: Is American democracy at odds with the traditions of the Catholic Church, or consonant with them?
answer_strings: Some have been grossly wronged by Latin republics and therefore dislike all republics. But we beg leave to remind these haters of all republics that we owe no thanks for our Constitution or Supreme Court to Jean Jacques Rousseau. We owe some thanks for our Constitution to principles of liberty and justice preserved by England from the Catholic Middle Ages in the face of the absolutism of the Reformation and the French Revolution.

We American Catholics recognize that this security for our Catholic liberties and our Catholic property has been a great cause of our religious progress, and we long for the day when Catholics in all other lands will have a Supreme Court like ours ever ready to protect them, as it has stood ever ready to protect us for over a hundred years.

Protestantism has the task of maintaining a free church within a free state. The great majority of Protestant people believe that parochialism is not good public policy for the following reasons: (a) The universal adoption of the parochial school system would make it difficult, if not impossible, for the state to guarantee that all the children in the nation would be taught the common elements necessary for the social solidarity of the people and the perpetuity of our democratic institutions.

The Roman Catholic Church, as a transnational hierarchy claiming spiritual sovereignty, historically views the secular state with guarded ambivalence, seeking concordats to safeguard her divine institutional rights; in contrast, Protestantism—particularly in its Calvinist and Anglo-American traditions—tends to view the democratic order as a natural extension of individual conscience and the priesthood of all believers.

The Church, teaching that authority derives from God and is held in trust for the common good, has ever been the champion of the people against the absolutism of princes--it was Bellarmine and Suarez, not Luther, who taught that sovereignty resides in the community--and the Catholic citizen, being schooled in a natural law that binds ruler and ruled alike, brings to the ballot box not the caprice of the hour but a settled conviction that there are things no majority may lawfully do.

If it is a corporation or association, we submit to the court that it is necessary for the Roman Catholic Church to allege specifically its incorporation, where incorporated, and by virtue of what authority or law it was incorporated, and if a foreign corporation, show that it has filed its articles of incorporation or association in the proper office of the government in accordance with the laws of Porto Rico.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a trial for arson and burglary before the Supreme Court of Massachusetts in 1834; the speeches of counsel and testimony of witnesses were published in Boston. The defendant was accused of breaking into an Ursuline Convent with 11 others; after the break-in, a mob burnt the convent.
main_question: How might counsel for the defense begin their summary remarks to the jury?
answer_strings: It has been said that the members of this Nunnery are called sisters of charity. I do not know that this was intended to create a prejudice, but we think this description of them is incorrect. I did not come here to speak against this institution; but if the government attempt to represent it as an institution of charity, we have a different view of it to present. If we are correct in our reading, nothing should alarm us more than the increase and prosperity of the Catholic religion. It is on the increase here, and this requires that its principles should be investigated.

Gentlemen of the jury, you stand today as the final rampart protecting an innocent man from being made the scapegoat for the passions of a violent night. The Commonwealth has presented you with a tragedy, but it has failed to present you with proof that this defendant committed the specific acts of arson and burglary charged against him. Disgust at the destruction of the Ursuline Convent must not blind us to the foundational principle of our republic: that guilt is individual, not collective, and must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. My client did not set those fires, nor did he break those doors, and no amount of public outrage can transform mere presence near a tumultuous crowd into criminal intent.

Gentlemen of the jury, the question before you is not whether an unlawful multitude assembled at Charlestown, nor whether the convent was afterwards consumed by fire; these facts are unhappily beyond dispute. The question is whether this defendant has been proved, by competent and certain testimony, to have joined in the breaking and entering charged in the indictment. He is not answerable for the passions of a mob merely because he was seen among a crowd, nor for the crime of others because public indignation demands a victim. You must separate suspicion from proof, and the tumult of that disastrous night from the individual guilt of the prisoner at the bar.

Gentlemen of the jury: you are asked to send to the state prison a Charlestown man, a laboring man, one of your own neighbors, and you are asked to do it chiefly upon the oaths of persons who are not of us, who owe their obedience to a foreign superior. Consider what manner of house that was upon Mount Benedict--a house whose walls no selectman of this town might pass without leave asked and granted. You have seen the Lady Superior in that chair, gentlemen; you have marked the temper in which she answered the questions put to her. I do not ask you to say the fire was well kindled; I ask you to say that the Commonwealth has not proved that this man kindled it, and to remember that the jury was planted in our law precisely so that no freeman should be delivered over to the resentment of an offended power upon evidence such as you have heard here.

The counsel for the government have offered evidence as to a nickname; but they failed to show it was fixed on the prisoner before that night; and if it had been, it amounts to nothing; for if a person was there for the purpose of destroying the Convent, he would be very likely to assume a name that would cast suspicion on some one else. The prisoner's character in New Hampshire, where he was born, is good. He has there a wife and five children. His life and character are now at stake; they are to depend on the imported testimony of Buck and Logan; and he appeals to you with confidence to say that such evidence as this is not to rob his children of their father and protector.
reject_reasons: uses a formula "beyond a reasonable doubt" that was not yet standard in instructions to juries (also, it neglects to consider the anti-Catholicism prevalent in Massachusetts at the time); overall, rather bad fit for the context of 1834.
is pretty good, and expressed in language appropriate for the period, but still neglects to consider that anti-Catholicism is an important lever giving the defense advantage.

while very good, and based in real historical context, doesn't quite nail the rhetorical strategy a lawyer would use in this period. This passage grasps that anti-Catholicism is an important resource for the defense. But it's too obvious in some ways (blaming a "foreign superior" -- the Pope -- who is not relevant to the case), and too subtle in other ways (being afraid to name the Catholic religion and directly say it's at issue).

metadata_frame: The following question is based on Ecce Cœlum; or Parish Astronomy, a popular science book published in 1867 by E. F. Burr, an American pastor from Connecticut, born in 1818. The best answer will respond as that book might have.
main_question: What is the use of astronomy?
answer_strings: We need to be trained to refined distinctions, to subtle analyses, to acuteness of thought; and for this purpose other sciences will answer better than astronomy. But we also need, still more, culture in breadth and dignity and gravity of ideas, in comprehension and solidity of understanding, in elevation and durable glow of imagination and character; and, for this purpose, no branch of secular knowledge can compare with the science of the stars. This science is worth more than all the fictions and poems in the world as a judicious cultivator of the imagination and corrector of insipidity and tameness of character.

But, after all, the most interesting and useful thing about astronomy is the illustration it pours on the attributes and glory of the Supreme Being. Let it be repeated, that ancient sentiment, "An undevout astronomer is mad." If one can thoughtfully pace up and down the star-sown fields of astronomy and not conceive a feeling of religious awe, as in the presence of Incomprehensible Almightiness, he must be a rare man, a sinner above all the Galileans. The fullest force of this inspired saying, "for the invisible things of Him are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and godhead,"--I say, the fullest force of these words is only felt by him whose thoughts, leaving the diminutive objects of this world, have gone voyaging through the inexhaustible wonders of the firmament.

The magnitudes, distances, arrangement, and motions of the great bodies which make up the visible universe, their constitution and physical condition, so far as they can be known to us, with their mutual influences and actions on each other, so far as they can be traced by the effects produced , and established by legitimate reasoning, form the assemblage of objects to which the attention of the astronomr is directed.

By the latest improvements in their instruments, astronomers have been enabled to note, with an incredible degree of precision, the apparent planes of the fixed stars and planets. As the accuracy of astronomical observation increased, the errors of the ancient theories exhibited themselves more clearly, and the mind of man has been enabled to explain, on sound and natural principles, the new phenomena which they have revealed. The discovery of the aberration of light and of the nutation of the earth's axis, two of the greatest discoveries of any age, have thus resulted.

It were a poor estimate of this science which reckoned only its services to the mariner; yet these are not to be despised, since without the lunar tables and the labours of the Nautical Almanac our commerce could not traverse the globe with that security which it now enjoys, nor could the surveyor fix his meridian, nor the railway its hour. But the higher utility of astronomy lies in its discipline of the mind, which it accustoms to patient observation and to the rejection of every conclusion not warranted by measurement; and in these latter years the spectroscope has taught us that the substances of the remotest suns are those we handle in our laboratories, a fact which no man could have predicted, and which enlarges our conception of the unity and constancy of the Creator's works.

The contemplation of the starry host is no mere secular pastime, but a sacred exercise that lifts the immortal soul to behold the unsearchable order, majesty, and mathematical precision of the Divine Architect. By mapping the immutable courses of the heavens, astronomy not only guides the humble mariner safely through the perils of the deep, but continuously humbles human pride before the boundless expanse of Jehovah’s creation. He who has once traced the path of a comet, or attended through a winter's night to the transit of a star, will not readily be persuaded that the universe is a thing of chance.

Suppose two lines drawn from the earth's center to opposite sides of the moon; then the real diameter of the moon makes with these a triangle. Now measure the moon's apparent diameter, which is the angle included between the supposed lines. The lines are about 240,000 miles each; the angle is about 31'. Then the simplest sort of mathematics gives you two thousand one hundred and sixty miles for the required diameter.
