metadata_frame: The following question is based on the 1868 volume of Friends' Review, a Quaker periodical published in Philadelphia. Good answers will approximate the likely perspective of that source.
main_question: Describe interactions between the US Government and Indian tribes toward the end of the 1860s.
answer_strings: The readers of the Review have been to a limited extent informed of the manner in which the officers of our government have been treating the Indians, but not a tenth of the inhuman, atrocious barbarities committed by the officers and soldiers of the government, and which are on file and record in the Indian Department in Washington, has been told them. The community have heard so much of war and bloodshed during the last few years that they have become callous to reports of outrage and cruelty which would have excited them under other circumstances; although they have heard but very little of the wholesale slaughter of hundreds of defenceless, innocent Indian women and children who were confiding in the protection of the very military forces by whom they were murdered.

In Third month last our government enacted a law prohibiting the President, Secretary of the Interior, and Commissioner of Indian Affairs, from making peace with any of the Indian tribes. This is one of the most extraordinary enactments that ever disgraced the history of any people. The meaning of this law was, that the Indians must yield or be exterminated, and the practical interpretation given to the law by the military, was, that after they had yielded, they were liable to be treated as belligerents still, and liable to be exterminated. For there was no treaty-making power lodged anywhere—not even with the highest military officers, who were campaigning against the Indians.

The internal struggle which the red man necessarily undergoes in adopting the resolution to throw away the blanket, the scalping-knife, and the implements of the chase, and, in lieu thereof, to wear a dress and devote himself to pursuits which he has been taught to consider degrading, is terrible; and if he emerges from it victorious, he becomes a new man. Wherever separate farms have been assigned within the limits of a tribal reservation to individual Indians, and the owners have entered into possession, a new life is apparent, comparative plenty is found on every hand, contentment reigns at every fireside, and peace and order have succeeded to turbulence and strife.

The history of the first missionary activities within the region in question began and ended within a period of seventy years. They could not be called successful in regard to immediate results, because the missionaries accomplished little because of the hostility of the Indians and of the protracted inter-tribal warfare. Their work was not in vain, however. The tradition of the Black-Robe, the name given to the missionaries by the Indians, continued to live in the hearts of the Indians, as the missionaries testified in their accounts of labors among the Northwest Indians.

We view with heavy hearts the dark and painful policies of our government, which continues to substitute the sword of force for the gentle spirit of Christian charity in its dealings with our Native brethren. While the peace policy entrusted to our friends offers a ray of hope for just and humane stewardship, the relentless encroachment of white settlers and the military's harsh measures threaten to extinguish every spark of mutual trust. If our nation is ever to escape the righteous judgment of Heaven, we must instantly abandon this course of coercion and honor our solemn treaties with unyielding honesty and love.

It is much to be regretted that, under the late act of Congress, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs was not permitted to seek a peaceful adjustment directly with the disaffected tribes, this duty being committed to a special commission in which the military element largely prevailed. Thus, while the representatives of the Government professed a desire to bury the hatchet, the accustomed instruments of war were still kept prominently before the Indian. Had upright and peaceable men been authorized to meet him in a spirit of justice, faithfully fulfilling former engagements and patiently hearing his complaints, much bloodshed might, we believe, have been averted.
reject_reasons: is more critical of "the red man" than typical for a Quaker periodical, and recommends a civilizing process that is less specifically Christianizing than one might expect

is clearly a history rather than a journalistic account of recent events, and the reference to Black-Robe suggests that it may also be written from a Catholic rather than Quaker point of view; not at all a good fit

is too abstract to be authentic; no specific events are described; also there is an adjectival prolixity (heavy hearts, harsh measures) that suggests 2020s cliche rather than an authentic 1860s source

is plausible in its advocacy of peaceful and just treatment, but more restrained than authentic sources from this period. It misrepresents the law as transferring negotiations to a special commission. Authentic Quaker accounts stress that the enactment lodged treaty-making authority nowhere and interpret this not as bureaucratic mismanagement but as an explicit policy of submission or extermination
manual_comment: The Friends' Review is consistently critical of the government; note also that "third month last" is a Quaker phrase.
source_title: Friends' Review; a Religious, Literary and Miscellaneous Journal

metadata_frame: The following question is based on the 1868 volume of Friends' Review, a Quaker periodical published in Philadelphia.
main_question: Write a sentence using the word "priesthood" that could have appeared in the specified context.
answer_strings: It would need no human priesthood, state-church, or salaried ministry, to induce the people to respect religion, or to speak well of His name, if it were the principal work of his followers in the world at large, to clothe the naked, feed the hungry, extend the hand of fellowship to the stranger or alien, visit the sick, and comfort those that are imprisoned and cast down!
We had no human priesthood, and did not admit that a man once a Minister must always be a Minister, far less that once an Elder he must always be an Elder.

The priesthood is therefore not merely an office created for convenience by the congregation, but a divine ministry entrusted with the preaching of the Word, the administration of the sacraments, the pronouncing of absolution, and the pastoral care of Christ’s flock.
Now, if we consider the subject, we shall see that the Sacraments answer most fully to the definition of a Priesthood, as given in my outset, except so far as they are acts, and not persons.

In remote times, men had nothing else with which to explore the heavens: but this, with the help of the pure Chaldean air and leisurely shepherd life; this, with the help of the perpetually cloudless Egyptian sky and the free, secluded life of the cultured and inquisitive priesthood, was sufficient to lay the foundations of astronomy.

It is not, we apprehend, by the setting apart of a separate order of men that the churches are edified; for the priesthood of the gospel is the priesthood of all believers, and the anointing which they have received of Him abideth in them, so that they need not that any man teach them, save as the Head of the Church is pleased to make one member serviceable to another.
reject_reasons: is virtually the opposite of Quaker belief.
uses the word more favorably and affirmatively than is typical in a Quaker context.
uses the word more favorably and affirmatively than is typical in a Quaker context.

takes the wrong side of a Quaker schism; it grounds its universal priesthood in 1 John 2:27 ("they need not that any man teach them") rather than the "royal priesthood" of 1 Peter 2:9 that Friends' Review actually favored as a target, and aims its polemic inward at Friends who would set apart an order — making it a quietist brief against the Gurneyite program this periodical existed to advance
manual_comment: This questions gets at the difference between Quaker beliefs and other varieties of Christian reliigious organization.
source_title: Friends' Review; a Religious, Literary and Miscellaneous Journal

metadata_frame: The following question is based on The Ladies' Repository, an American periodical published in Boston in 1857.
main_question: Provide a substantial, three-sentence description of the appearance and dress of a female character who might appear in a story published in the specified context.
answer_strings: She was a dear little woman, she had the prettiest hands and arms in the world, and they were well shown off by the fall of rich lace about the sleeves. I had always admired her hair, and it was arranged as becomingly as ever. She wore a silk dress which fitted her slender waist to perfection, the skirt was made of little ruffles of silk flowing out very wide at the bottom, so that when she sat down, she covered quite an area of carpet, and then growing smaller and beautifully less at the top.

Mary was a brunette, with strongly marked features, her eyes large and black as night, and hair to match them. She was tall, a good figure, very erect, her head set rather proudly upon her shoulders, and now there was an unusual color upon her cheek, that gave her additional beauty. Her dress was a black velvet jacket over a white skirt , and a light scarf of crimson silk wound among the braids of her black hair, gave quite a gypsy-like air to her whole appearance.

Her dark hair was neatly parted in the center and drawn smoothly over her temples into a tight chignon, framing a pale, refined countenance marked by thoughtful dark eyes and a demeanor of quiet composure. She wore a fitted bodice of deep indigo silk featuring wide pagoda sleeves that flared at the elbows to reveal delicate, lace-trimmed undersleeves of white lawn. Her broad, bell-shaped skirt was supported by heavy crinoline petticoats and draped gracefully to the floor in soft folds, reflecting both the modest propriety and functional elegance characteristic of a young woman of her station.

She was a slight and graceful girl, with a clear pale complexion, large hazel eyes shaded by dark lashes, and a profusion of glossy brown hair parted smoothly upon her forehead and gathered in heavy braids behind. Her dress was of a soft gray merino, made high in the neck and close in the sleeves, with a narrow white collar and cuffs, while a small brooch of dark enamel formed its only ornament. There was nothing striking or costly in her attire, yet the neatness of every fold, the delicacy of her hands, and the quiet composure of her manner gave her an air of refinement which richer apparel might only have obscured.

Where her journey began, where it ended, he had never bothered himself to inquire. It satisfied his needs to expect her at such a time each day and to realize his expectations. Her hair burned like a copper-beech in the sunshine, and her face was as white as milk.

At last the bride made her appearance. Emmeline was nineteen. She was slightly formed, had a most winning countenance, innocent laughing eyes, and a delicate, fair complexion, although now deepened into crimson, in her cheeks, by the agitation of the moment, as was very apparent, even through the folds of the beautiful lace veil that hung all over her.

She wore purple; not an old woman's purple, but a soft shade which did not take from her youth. There was something floating round her shoulders of the same colour, and on her arms were long gloves such as you see our young ladies wear. The child did not seem to belong to her, though she held her tightly by the hand.
reject_reasons: has a self-conscious ethnographic character; it seems sometimes to be illustrating generalizations about social structure in this period rather than describing a character; probably composed in some later era
is fairly plausible, and yet, doesn't have quite as much detail about dress as we might expect in a publication like The Ladies' Repository
is too modern and too wryly cynical for the 1850s context; also, perhaps, too centered on the perceptions of a masculine observer for the periodical in question
touches only lightly on physical details, and seems for that reason more likely to be a passage from 1820s silver-fork fiction than the detail-rich realist fiction of mid-century
has a loose, impressionist approach to description that seems much later than the 1850s, almost modernist
manual_comment: The ground truth answers come from two different stories by different authors in the same volume of this periodical.

metadata_frame: The following question is drawn from Marrying Is Not a Brilliant Joke, a newspaper column published in 1928 by May Edginton, a British novelist.
main_question: Write two sentences of advice for young people thinking of getting married that we might expect to find in the specified context.
answer_strings: Make your marriage carefully. Be sure either of its finances or your own strength.
Without good health, consider the duty and responsibility of children very carefully. With good health, consider the arid and bleak condition of childlessness even more carefully.

Neither physical nor mental health can follow a marriage that takes place too early. It is almost impossible to make a right choice, and the constitution is not well enough formed to bear the great physical changes that usually occur.
The person you marry comes as is. You should not expect to control or change them, and that’s what dating is for, to see if you want to sign up with a person just the way they are.

Single persons who desire the personal marriage, ascribe an undue amount of loneliness to the lack of the domestic companionship they long for. It is the inner marriage which drives away loneliness, the loving to do real service in the world.

Before stepping to the altar, remember that a enduring marriage requires as much sensible patience and joint budgeting as it does romantic sentiment. Choose a partner whose character you respect in times of hardship, for love thrives best when grounded in common ideals, mutual loyalty, and hard work.

And this brings us back, as everything does, to the matter of the salary. A young man who cannot support himself in comfort will not be able to support two in comfort merely by the addition of a wife, though the arithmetic of courtship somehow persuades a good many of them otherwise.
reject_reasons: has a gravity of tone that would be out of place in a newspaper column, and also is offering advice with a euphemistic delicacy that seems to come from earlier than the 1920s, possibly even mid-19c
sounds much later than the 1920s, in its diction and in its confidence that marriage will be preceded by a number of trial relationships
sounds more religious or spiritual than we would expect from a newspaper column by a novelist

has a rhetorical closure that gives it away as composed synthetically by a language model specifically in answer to this question: note, for instance, the way it ends on a tricolon; also its language for financial management was not common before the late 20c

has the wryness we'd expect from a column, and suggests real embeddedness by referring to a preceding argument; diction is also plausibly 1920s; is maybe just slightly more conservative than actual late-1920s advice?
manual_comment: A classic question, where it's possible to find real advice from different periods and from different genres.
source_title: Marrying Is Not a Brilliant Joke

metadata_frame: The following question is drawn from records of appeals before a British judge of the East India Company's district (zillah) court at Chicacole, in the Madras Presidency, deciding civil appeals from Indian subordinate judges in April 1853.
main_question: Consider the following appeal, and write a short paragraph expressing the British judge's likely response. 1. Appellant states - He sued the Respondents to obtain possession of a house and site valued at 16 rupees; which case the Sudr Ameen examined, and dismissed his claim, and ordered each party to pay their own costs: with which being dissatisfied he brought this appeal. 2. Appeal reasons--Independent of the admission of the Respondents , he proved by evidence that this house and site belonged to him; whereas, the Sudr Ameen passed his decree in favor of the Respondents on the single evidence for defence. This property was not given by him to the Respondents on any conditions, nor was a promise held out by him on the subject. He therefore prays the Court to confirm his claim.
answer_strings: The Court finds, though there is no doubt that the site belongs to the Appellant, still he gave the Respondents leave to build their house on it, and though there is only one witness who corroborates the statement of the Respondents, that they were to return the site when they left it, and might live there as long as they wished to do so, the Civil Judge cannot see that the Sudr Ameen could even, on this one evidence's corroboration, do otherwise than say, he considered they had a right to keep possession, which they had done for so many years undisturbed, and it would in his opinion, be a very dangerous precedent to dispossess parties of a house, on the caprice of any party, for offences taken or conceived on a moment's notice, where there are no documents on either side. He therefore confirms the Lower Court's decree, and dismisses the appeal with costs.

The proceedings of the Sudder Ameen having been perused, this Court sees no ground for disturbing his decision. The Appellant, being out of possession, was bound to establish his title by clear proof, and has failed to do so; his witnesses speak to general repute rather than to any act of ownership within their knowledge, and are contradicted upon the material point by the testimony for the defence, which the Sudder Ameen, having had the parties before him, was competent to believe. As to the admission relied on, an admission cannot be received in part and rejected in part: the Respondents, while allowing that the site was formerly the Appellant's, allege in the same breath that it was made over to them and has since been built upon and held undisturbed, and the Appellant, who took no step during that period, cannot now sever the acknowledgment from the qualification accompanying it. The decree of the Sudder Ameen is confirmed, and this appeal dismissed, with costs upon the Appellant.

The Civil Judge sees no reason to interfere with the decision of the lower court. The Appellant having failed to produce any clear documentary title or unexceptionable evidence of his exclusive ownership, the Sudr Ameen was fully justified in crediting the defense witness and finding that the Appellant had not established a valid claim to eject the occupants. Where an original plaintiff relies upon disputed oral testimony to dispossess established occupants, the onus of proving clear title rests entirely on him; as the Appellant failed to discharge this burden, the decree of the Sudr Ameen is affirmed, and this appeal is dismissed with costs.

The Respondents’ own admission, supported by the evidence adduced by the Appellant, sufficiently establishes his title to the house and site; while the single witness for the defence affords no adequate ground for rejecting his claim. The decree of the Sudr Ameen is therefore reversed, and possession of the property is awarded to the Appellant, with costs in both Courts.

On examining the record, the Court finds the Respondent, in original plaint, requested to recover lands producing 40 rupees, and past produce 24 rupees. The Court considers a full enquiry necessary in order to do justice and pass a proper decree, and therefore remands the suit to the Moonsiff, directing him to examine the witnesses of Appellant, and then pass a decree on full merits, including these costs in the new decree according to the Circular Order of the Sudr Udalut dated 12th February 1844.
reject_reasons: is actually pretty good; it errs perhaps by being too formal and legal, since this court was not bound by formal legal doctrine--e.g. that admissions are indivisible--as much as by prudential considerations.
errs perhaps by being too formal and legal, since this court was not bound by formal legal doctrine as much as by prudential considerations
is not actually a probable response to this case. In the absence of documentary evidence, judges were reluctant to dispossess inhabitants.
does not seem to be responding to this case, but to a different case about agricultural produce; bad context fit.
manual_comment: Explores understanding of colonial justice.
source_title: Decisions, Zillah. Subordinante [and Assistant] Courts, Madras Presidency

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a collection of aphorisms and practical maxims published in 1929 by Fred Van Amburgh, an American editor born in 1866. Answers should approximate aphorisms that could have appeared in such a collection.
main_question: Write an aphorism about advertising.
answer_strings: The force of advertising largely depends upon the amount of powder put behind it. Advertising is like a bombardment, its effectiveness depends upon keeping it up.
Sometimes it does not pay to advertise and here is your proof: A firm advertised in the Monday evening papers for a night watchman, and before morning the safe was robbed.
From any cross-section of ads, the general advertiser's attitude would seem to be: if you are a lousy, smelly, idle, underprivileged and oversexed status-seeking neurotic moron, give me your money.
Advertising is a valuable economic factor because it is the cheapest way of selling goods, particularly if the goods are worthless.

Selling the advertising in a country newspaper is really the big moneymaking department, and to build this up, the owner will find a man "whose head is full of ideas and who seems born to sell newspaper advertising."

The advertising man should study his readers with great consideration. Advertising, in a sense, may be defined as the influence of mind over mind, therefore the psychological element in advertising is a most important one.
Advertising is the modern substitute for reputation: what a man's neighbours once said of him, he now says of himself, and in larger type.

When little Timmy returned from the country with a dreadful rash, his mother immediately credited the radio announcer's glowing pitch for the local sulfur bath soap. Her husband merely adjusted his spectacles over the morning paper and observed that if advertisement could make a tub of foul water sound like the Fountain of Youth, it was high time they bought stock in the mud factory.
reject_reasons: is perceptibly anachronistic; e.g. "status-seeking" is a concept that doesn't become common until the 1950s; its firm negativism toward advertising is also out of place in the 1920s
is more bitterly negative about advertising than usual in the 1920s
doesn't feel like an aphorism; it's just a random sentence that mentions advertising, so it fails on the genre dimension of context
sounds like practical advice rather than an aphorism, so it fails the genre dimension of context

is too perfectly epigrammatic for the casual 1920 balanced antithesis — "the art of saying loudly what would not be believed if said quietly," "what his neighbours once said of him, he now says of himself" — is Wildean epigram, and it is period-marked to the 1890s
is a humorous anecdote, but not exactly an aphorism
manual_comment: This not only tests attitudes about advertising, but the tone of humor in the 1920s.

metadata_frame: Answers to the following question were drawn from a range of books published in the United States toward the end of the 1920s. The ideal answer will approximate a passage that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: Write two or three sentences about marriage.
answer_strings: The willingness to try and understand the true aims and ambitions of your co-partner is indeed an important idea, but a more necessary rule is to not get so confounded serious, sober and solemn when things go wrong. Life partnership is based on happiness, and the sense of humor is sure to save so much unhappiness.

Nowadays girls of sixteen are kept from marriage and other useful occupations by compulsory education. Not so in the dark sixties. At sixteen girls were considered capable of fulfilling the two roles then assigned to them--matrimony and the instruction of the young.

What greater thing is there for two human souls, than to feel that they are joined for life — to strengthen each other in all labour, to rest on each other in all sorrow, to minister to each other in all pain, to be one with each other in silent unspeakable memories at the moment of the last parting?
Marriage isn't all that it's cracked up to be. Let me tell you, honestly. Marriage is probably the chief cause of divorce.

Adultery, with all its evils and its shocking incompatibility with our morals, is at last only a reassertion of the imprescriptible rights of personal liberty, which marriage pretends to alienate by mortgage. It is undoubtedly a morbid, social symptom, but it is a reactive symptom, and indicates a vital tendency to escape the compression of the paralysing marriage form.

A good marriage remains the quiet bedrock of society, where a woman gracefully tempers her husband's ambition with home-front order, ensuring the sanctuary of the parlor stays untroubled by the world's anxieties. Though modern times permit her a brief measure of independence outside the home, her highest duty is still understood to be the delicate art of making his return feel like the ultimate reward.
They say marriage is a lottery. It is nothing of the kind. In a lottery a man has some chance of getting his money back, and nobody expects him to keep on buying the same ticket.
reject_reasons: has a solemnity and a grandiloquence out of place in the later 1920s; it comes from an earlier period
sounds more like dialogue than book text, and "cracked up to be" reaches peak popularity later than the 1920s
is perceptibly earlier than the 1920s, both in its moralism and its diction; e.g. "imprescriptible," and this particular sense of the verb "alienate"; in fact it comes from the 1850s
is perceptibly later than the 1920s; the phrase "home-front" is endemic to the 1940s; also, it's a tissue of clichés and feels synthetic
is a little unlikely to have been written in the 1920s, since lotteries had been illegal for some time in the US at that point; however it must be admitted this is a strong option
manual_comment: The second passage comes from Frank Norris, by Charles Dobie, 1928. The only context really being tested here is period context, and perhaps localization to the US.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on The Thought Arouser, a collection of practical maxims and aphorisms published in 1929 by Fred Van Amburgh, an American editor. Answers should ideally be passages that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: Write a practical maxim about good salesmanship.
answer_strings: In selling, the mistake is often made of talking too much. Arguments seldom sell. Debates are dangerous. The power of suggestion often proves more successful.
To "push over" an undecided customer may be a mark of smart salesmanship, but it is also a high-pressure, slapstick scheme that in the end will do the seller more harm than good.
The third great pitfall in the path of the young salesman is card-playing . There is always, when traveling, an opportunity to sit in a game of poker. It is a bad habit.
Great salespeople are relationship builders who provide value and help their customers win.
A successful salesman never sells the cold iron of the stove, but the warm comfort of the family kitchen, for a prospect buys not the object itself, but the feeling of prosperity it promises.

A man may be talked into one purchase by sheer persistence, and the traveller enters it in his book and counts the day well spent. But no house was ever built upon triumphs of that description. Go back in six months. If the shopkeeper comes forward to meet you at the door, you have made a connexion; if he finds sudden business at the far end of the counter, you have made a sale. The one is capital; the other is petty cash.
reject_reasons: doesn't fit the generic context of a collection of maxims; 'third great pitfall' sounds like part of a more connected exposition
relies on the concept of a "relationship builder" which would be anachronistic in the 1920s; it's a later twentieth century concept
strongly resembles the advice in a 1937 book of advice for salesmen--"don't sell the steak, sell the sizzle!" But that book would not exist yet in 1929; this is subtly anachronistic in that context.
uses a British idiom (connexion, of that description) that is out of place in our 1929 American target context
manual_comment: Salesmanship is a very 1920s concept.

metadata_frame: Answers to the following question should resemble a passage that could have been written in the 1880s; but within that constraint, a wide range of genres and perspectives are imaginable.
main_question: What might a writer in the specified period predict about social, philosophical, or technical changes in the future? Write two or three sentences making a prediction about the future that wouldn't seem out of place in the period's writing.
answer_strings: The action of the voltaic current also decomposes water, setting free its component gases, the combustible hydrogen, and the supporter of combustion, oxygen. And may we not anticipate that in the not far distant future that water will be used as our combustible material. When that takes place, water in the form of steam will cease to be the power, and water itself will be the substitute.

The notion that the uncounted millions whose maximum of faculty is below the conditions of civilized character are, "under the law," disobedient in a sense and degree to merit unending misery, would seem grotesque, did it not wear the worse character of being barbarian. The notion that justice may rightfully consign the whole family of mankind to hopeless perdition, with the exception of those so fortunate as to be fools or infants, will, I doubt not, in a future age be cited as a proof that even the nineteenth century had not fully emerged from the ages characterized as the "dark."

As the subterranean pneumatic tubes and galvanic wires weave an ever-denser web beneath our bustling thoroughfares, it requires little imagination to foresee an age when human speech shall be transmitted instantly across oceans, rendering physical distance a mere phantom of the past. Yet one must ponder whether this relentless acceleration of intercourse will truly elevate the human spirit, or merely deliver us into a state of perpetual nervous agitation, where the quiet contemplation essential to philosophy is forever drowned by the clamor of the world.

The time may not be distant when electricity, already the swift messenger of our thoughts, shall become the common servant of every household, supplying light, heat, and mechanical power at a trifling cost. With easier communication between nations and a wider diffusion of knowledge, many ancient distinctions of class may gradually lose their force, though it would be rash to suppose that increased material comfort will of itself render mankind either wiser or more virtuous.

Steam, however, is pushing its inexorable way into these hitherto excluded regions, and unless nature be proof against art, bids fair soon to change the manner of their inhabitants, and to make the Arab, after he has withstood innovation for more than 4,000 years, acknowledge its power-a power that will attack him by reducing his isolation, and subdue his independence by multiplying his physical wants-with what result to his happiness the future will reveal; only he has no choice between courting the new agent of his destiny or being driven out of existence by it.

The Volapükists are laughed at by practical men, yet they have seized the true tendency of the age: a century which has abolished distance by the electric wire will not long submit to the barbarism of a hundred tongues. And when a speech purged of those irregularities which are but the fossil remains of savage habits of mind has become the common possession of Europe and her colonies, we may look for a corresponding rectitude in thought itself; for error is propagated chiefly through the ambiguities of the vulgar languages, and a people that cannot say a confused thing will in time cease to think one.

There is, however, good reason to hope that if the light of knowledge continues to increase in our world, narrow orthodoxies in both science and religion will in time disappear. Just as we have seen narrow orthodoxies in religion breaking up in our own day, so probably a not distant future will see the disappearance of tendencies to narrow orthodoxies in science. For men, if allowed to think freely, will see that the scientific spirit is the open-minded love of truth and is quite independent of the straight-jacket of any method.
reject_reasons: is overdetermined; yes the Victorians did have telegraphs and envision pneumatic tubes, but this reads a little too much as contemporary hand-wringing about the information age projected backward onto the 19c; it lacks the quality of randomness that distinguishes authentic period futurism

is a bit too much on the nose; the second industrial revolution in the early 20c did depend on electrification, and writers of the 1880s were certainly fascinated by electricity; but a paragraph that mixes electrification with unspecified communication advances and class leveling is suspiciously prescient; this was likely written by LLM

is somewhat plausible for the 1880s, although the particular technical advances described here are not really new in the 1880s, which together with slightly fussy syntax, offers a clue that the source of this passage may be mid-19c, not 1880s

is better than some, since it avoids the trap of predicting our own future, and chooses instead a vogue for artificial languages that was distinctive of the 1880s; it slips however by caricaturing the period's progressivism and rationalism

expresses a confidently universalizing rationalism that would still have been shocking in the 1880s, and does so in plain language that sounds more like the 1920s or 1930s; was probably not really written in the target period
manual_comment: Very open-ended question; there is no one right answer, and partial credit has been provided. But there are clear ways to go wrong here, and one is to make a prediction that leans too heavily on our retrospective interest in *being predicted*. Note that the ground truth sources are HN1LS2 and 32044088989421, while partial credit comes from 32044103077657 in 1860.
source_title: The System of Calculating Diameter, Circumference, Area, and Squaring the Circle : Together With Interest and Miscellaneous Tables, and Other Information

metadata_frame: The following question is drawn from Lessons in Modern Farming; or, Agriculture for Schools, a collection of essays on agriculture published in 1851 by John Lauris Blake, an American clergyman and author.
main_question: Write a sentence using the word "energy" that also mentions soil or compost, and would be likely to be found int the specified context.
answer_strings: Science, as in other departments of knowledge, came to our relief, demonstrating the self-sustaining energy of the soil to all the purposes for which it was designed, provided we keep it under the dominion of those physical laws which govern material nature.

It is clear that here may be found a large amount of the roots of grasses and other decayed vegetable substances; here, too, have been deposited animal excrements; so that the entire sod is capable of being converted, in a well prepared compost heap, into a manure of great energy.
The general energy of growth on well-protected limy soil is also evidenced by strong reproductive capacity in coppice through stool-shoots and stoles, and by the long vitality of the stools.

It is shown that there is a close relationship with vegetation, the soil population being dependent almost entirely on the growing plant for energy material, while the plant is equally dependent on the activities of the soil population for removing the residues of previous generations of plants and for the continued production in the soil of simple materials, such as nitrates, which are necessary to its growth.

It is not enough that the muck-heap be carted out in March and spread over the sour swale; unless the farmer bring to that labor an energy proportioned to the stubbornness of a soil which has lain wet and unstirred since his father's time, his compost will lie unrotted till August, and the crop must answer for it.
By the judicious application of rich compost, the diligent husbandman restores to the weary soil that vital energy which successive harvests, all too commonly, have drained away.
The energy of the soil may be greatly increased by the liberal application of well-rotted compost, which enriches it with the elements of fertility and gives new vigor to the growing crop.

metadata_frame: The best answers to the following question will resemble passages that could have appeared in a book published for the first time in the 1850s; within that period, a range of different genres and contexts are possible.
main_question: Write a single sentence of at least thirty words that uses both the word "science" and the word "future," and that could have appeared in the specified period.
answer_strings: Who can look forward, through the long vista of time to come, and foretell what vast improvements future ages are destined to witness--what, upon this great theatre of action, freedom, and enterprise, science and industry are yet to accomplish?

I do not hereby mean to affirm that these bodies are really simple; for it is very possible that the future progress of science will enable us to effect decompositions which resist our present means; and then many, perhaps all, of the bodies now regarded as simple, will be found to be compound.

Let us here, however, pause for a moment, to express our earnest wish and humble hope that the great Disposer of events may approve of the motives of this assembly; that His blessing may rest upon the work; that He may render it, in our hands, subservient to the great and disinterested purposes of extensive utility, which it is its sole object to attain; and that in future times this edifice may be the glory of our children's children ; that commerce and science may here be entwined in perpetual friendship, uniting their strength for the glory of the empire, the stability of the throne, the perpetuity of our glorious constitution, and the prosperity of the people at large.

It is interesting at this stage to note that Signor Marconi, more fortunate than some famous inventors, surrounded himself with associates who had the foresight and imagination to picture the future possibilities of the new science.

As the modern world marvels at the swift advancement of steam navigation and magnetic telegraphy, the learned scholars of our age must humbly acknowledge that the true triumph of science lies in securing a more enlightened future for all mankind.

Whether the science of another age shall confirm or overthrow these conclusions, we do not presume to say; enough that they are honestly arrived at, and that the future has never yet dealt hardly with the man who reasoned according to his lights.

main_question: What is a flat file?
answer_strings: A flat file is identically the same as the box file in operation, but more convenient to handle. Each tray houses a section of the alphabet and is labeled on the front indicating its contexts.
A flat file is a plain text file that stores data in a structured, two-dimensional format (rows and columns) without any relational links, hierarchies, or complex indexing built into the file itself.

A flat file is a shallow cabinet or case of wide drawers used for storing maps, drawings, prints, plans, and other large sheets without folding them. The papers are laid flat in the drawers, both to keep them orderly and to prevent creasing or damage.

A flat file is a system of drawers where all correspondence to, from, or about an individual, firm, or subject is filed on edge, usually in folders and behind guides, making for speed, accuracy, and accessibility.
A "flat file" is a humorous euphemism for a system of records management where papers are simply laid flat on the surface of a desk, in piles, without structure or system.

metadata_frame: The best answer to the following question will approximate the perspective of a travel guide to Dorsetshire published in 1872, in Edinburgh.
main_question: Describe Lyme Regis.
answer_strings: He who goeth to Lyme Regis will find its inhabitants proud of three things,--their Esplanade, their Cobb or pier, and their George Inn." The first is a broad level walk by the sea-side, much frequented by nurserymaids, children, invalids, and young ladies in crinoline. The second shelters the sands from violent seas, and is really a curious and note-worthy structure.

The visitor must next direct his attention to the town's natural advantages-to the mighty hills that roll along the coast, like billow upon billow-to the abrupt peak of the RHODE HORN, rising in the rear of the town, and penetrated by the artificial cutting of the NEW PASSAGE: a breeze-swept road not to be lightly adventured upon in a winter gale-to the sands, level and tenacious; and the cliffs broken up into a thousand picturesque forms.

In the western part of Dorsetshire on the very confines of Devon, between and on the ascent of two romantic hills, at the deepest part of the West Bay, in longitude 3º 43' west  latitude 50 ° 48'north, is agreeably situated the ancient town of Lyme, which enjoys a climate eminently mild and salubrious, distant from London 143 miles, 24 from Dorchester, and 28 from Exeter. The lower part of the town is washed by the sea, from the violence of which it is protected by walls and jetties, while the environs are extremely rural and picturesque, abounding in romantic scenery.

Lyme Regis is a town in west Dorset, England, 25 miles west of Dorchester and east of Exeter. Sometimes dubbed the "Pearl of Dorset", it lies by the English Channel at the Dorset–Devon border. It has noted fossils in cliffs and beaches on the Jurassic Coast.

Perched delightfully upon the picturesque Dorset coast, Lyme Regis—the historic "Pearl of Dorset"—offers the discerning holidaymaker a most charming retreat from the bustle of modern town life. Here, quaint, winding streets lined with ancient stone cottages slope steeply down to the sea, where the famous Cobb—a ancient and magnificent stone pier—sweeps majestically out to shelter the harbour, just as it did in the romantic days of Jane Austen.

Lyme Regis, a picturesque watering-place situated on the rocky coast of Dorsetshire, is justly celebrated for its magnificent stone Cobb and the salubrious sea breezes that invigorate the summer visitor. The romantic observer and scientific natural-historian alike will find endless delight along its crumbling cliffs, where fossilized remains of ancient reptilian monsters are daily exposed by the action of the tides.

The square massive tower of the CHURCH (which is dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul) will attract the visitor's attention immediately upon his entrance into the town. The ground-plan of the building is cruciform, and the architecture Early English  but repairs and restorations have been recently made at a considerable expense, and with a questionable result. The most satisfactory building in the town is the ALMS HOUSE, erected from Mr. Francis ' designs, in 1843, in pursuance of the directions of the will of a Mr. William Clark.

LYME REGIS, a small but ancient borough and bathing-place in the county of Dorset, pleasantly seated in a hollow of the cliffs at the mouth of the Lym, and reached by coach from the Axminster station of the South-Western (6 m.); pop. about 2,000, the streets steep and narrow, the air mild and much commended for invalids, and the whole overlooked by that famous curving pier, the Cobb, from which the Duke of Monmouth's men came ashore in 1685, and whereon a lady of Miss Austen's novel suffered her celebrated fall.

metadata_frame: The following question is drawn from A Dissertation on the Varieties of Mankind : Being an Address Read Before the Cuvierian and Physiological Societies of Wesleyan University, a lecture delivered in 1843 by an American physician. The best answer will approximate the likely perspective of that document.
main_question: What evidence does craniology provide about differences between the races of mankind?
answer_strings: We cannot, in our present state of physiological knowledge, draw any fair conclusions with regard to mental capacity from peculiarities of cranial formation. We have by no means such satisfactory knowledge of the intellectual functions of the brain as to enable us to examine into its qualities by the simple process of mensuration.

Mr. Lawrence furnishes us with experimental evidence that his whole craniological system is unfounded; for the success of these very missionaries and Bible Societies has proved the moral capability of the negroes; it has proved that contrary opinions based upon physiological theories are erroneous, and the inference is strong that the assumed intellectual inferiority which is based upon the same foundation is equally visionary and untenable.

I place small faith in the bumps and organs which the phrenologists would read off a man's head; but Dr. Morton's gauging of the internal capacity, done with shot and scale, is another matter altogether, and the difference he finds between the Caucasian and the Ethiopian skull is not to be argued away.

While the ingenious craniologist seeks to divide the human family by measuring the cold, lifeless bone of the skull, Holy Scripture clearly reveals that God hath made of one blood all nations of men to dwell on all the face of the earth. We must beware lest these worldly classifications obscure the immortal soul within, which alone bears the equal image of its Creator regardless of outward form.

Gentlemen, the testimony of craniology, confirmed as I believe by comparative anatomy and the history of civilization, affords strong evidence that the races of mankind exhibit innate differences in cerebral development no less than in physical conformation. It is therefore difficult to resist the conclusion that those peoples who have attained the highest forms of social and industrial organization represent the more advanced stages of human evolution.

I am glad to find that this opinion is confirmed by Humboldt, and by the conclusions which Dr. M'Culloch has drawn , from a very extensive examination of what has been written on this subject. I have, therefore, no hesitation in adopting the opinion of the latter author, who acknowledges but three fixed distinctions of colour, the white, brown, and black, the rest being accidental tints, the result of climate, habit, and intermixture.

Craniology is the scientific study of the size, shape, and anatomical characteristics of the skull. It provides foundational knowledge for understanding human evolution, forensic identification, and the biomechanics of the head.
reject_reasons: places too much emphasis on racial difference for the context of a Northern university early in the 1840s. Also, while Morton had published in 1843 he was not yet widely popularized.
is too dogmatically pious for the context of an academic address by a physician in the 1840s.
is anachronistic, both in its support for racial difference and in its references to 'industrial organization' and 'human evolution.' Sounds later in the nineteenth century.
does not really address the question about craniology
doesn't address the question about human racial difference, but instead provides a strikingly modern definition of craniology, complete with an anachronistic reference to evolution
manual_comment: The frame provides the title in full, because Wesleyan University is a clue that we are in a Northern and consciously Christian context as well as an academic one. In the 1840s, monogenesis was still dominant.
source_title: A Dissertation on the Varieties of Mankind : Being an Address Read Before the Cuvierian and Physiological Societies of Wesleyan University

metadata_frame: In answering the following question, envision the context of Protestantism's Contribution to Character Building in a Democracy, a public address published in 1926 by Walter Athearn, an American professor of religious education. The best answers will approximate Athearn's perspective.
main_question: Why does the author believe Protestant and Catholic churches have a different relation to the secular democratic state?
answer_strings: Faced with the educational implications involved in the principle of the separation of church and state, the Catholic and Protestant churches in America have moved in opposite directions. The Catholic Church has the task of maintaining an autocratic church within a democratic state. It has been in America the chief proponent of the parochial school system.

Protestantism has the task of maintaining a free church within a free state. The great majority of Protestant people believe that parochialism is not good public policy for the following reasons: (a) The universal adoption of the parochial school system would make it difficult, if not impossible, for the state to guarantee that all the children in the nation would be taught the common elements necessary for the social solidarity of the people and the perpetuity of our democratic institutions.

The Reformation, in restoring to the individual conscience the right of private judgment and to the congregation the ordering of its own affairs, bred in our Anglo-Saxon stock precisely those habits of self-government which the republic afterward required of its citizens; the New England town meeting is but the church meeting carried out of doors. The Roman communion, by contrast, trains its people to receive doctrine and discipline from a hierarchy culminating in a foreign sovereign who has in our own generation declared himself infallible and condemned in the Syllabus the very liberties we hold dear --and a man schooled from childhood in such obedience can hardly be expected to bring to the ballot box the independent judgment upon which free institutions depend.

An age of science has given us a partial and incomplete view of nature. This partial and incomplete view of nature has been carried over into the fields of education, sociology, philosophy and religion. A materialistic age is the result.

The Roman Catholic Church, as a transnational hierarchy claiming spiritual sovereignty, historically views the secular state with guarded ambivalence, seeking concordats to safeguard her divine institutional rights; in contrast, Protestantism—particularly in its Calvinist and Anglo-American traditions—tends to view the democratic order as a natural extension of individual conscience and the priesthood of all believers.

Democracy is actually rooted in the core of Catholic doctrine: the divine dignity of the human soul, created in the image of God, and the sacred equality of all men before Him. Indeed, long before modern parliaments arose, the Church championed the fundamental principles that make a free society possible--specifically, the rule of law over arbitrary tyranny and the natural rights of the family and local communities, which no state may justly destroy.

For all the nation's clamor of creeds and sects, the sturdy habits of self-government have found their surest ally in the Protestant churches, whose congregations have long schooled Americans in the practice of democracy.

fails to address the question at all, and instead discusses science and materialism

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a treatise about ghosts and dreams published in 1841 by a British surgeon and writer forn in 1794. The best answers will approximate passages that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: Distinguish the different types of ghosts and phantasms.
answer_strings: In the first class there is no real or palpable object, or, if there be, it is not what it appears; the illusion is but the reality of romance, depending altogether on excited or disordered conditions of the mind: the source, therefore, either of bright or gloomy phantoms, as the mood may be. The second class, which are spectres or ghosts of the eye, may be scientifically explained by the laws which govern the material world. These are the only substantial ghosts which I can grant to my friend. The objects themselves exist, and are exactly as they appear.

Optical illusions will be doubled by a straining or altering of the axes of the eyes; and by turning round, as they are removed from the axis of vision, they will disappear. But in the purely metaphysical ghost or phantom, the change of position or locality will not essentially dispel the illusion (the spectrum following, as it were, the motion of the eye); because it exists in the mind itself, either as a faint or transient idea or a mere outline, fading perhaps in a brighter light, or as the more permanent and confirmed impression of insanity.

The representatives of these classes with which we shall chiefly have to deal are first, Fate; second, devils and angels, or in general figures embodying the good and evil impulses of humanity; third, witches (and in a subordinate degree magicians); and fourth, ghosts; with such examples of our third class as we may encounter and define. This may suffice as a general classification; since the several types make their appearance at various times, and under different conditions.

There are other types of ghosts with which the reader is no doubt familiar--the Banshee, the ghost attached to a particular family and appearing in the form of a wailing woman, the rustle of paper, a mouse, a white bird, or other portent, to give warning of impending death; the phantom carriage which rolls up the drive by the light of the winter's moon; the small dark spectres which haunt the Cornish mines; the black hound; the headless horseman; the phantom cavalcade. But stories of this kind for the most part rest upon tradition only, and seem to belong to folklore rather than to psychical research. In no case is the evidence at present obtained sufficient to justify detailed consideration.

In my rigorous observation of these mysterious phenomena, I have resolved all spectral manifestations into two grand classes: the Corporal Phantasm, which is but a mere optical deception birthed from a sluggish liver, a troubled brain, or an excess of black bile, and the True Astral Visitor, wherein a genuine spirit penetrates the mortal veil whilst the subject's soul lies in slumber. The former is no more than a trick of disordered physiology, readily banished by a brisk dose of calomel. The latter, however, belongs to the subtle mechanics of the invisible world--a sublime visitant whose mysterious laws no scalpel can dissect, nor any potion in the pharmacopoeia dispel.

Of phantasms I recognise three classes, and no more. The first are ocular merely--those spectra that swim upon the retina after the candle is snuffed. The second I name cerebral, being the dream that continues its business some minutes after the sleeper has quitted his bed, much as an amputated limb will persist in complaining of its toes. The third and by far the most numerous are the gastric: I hold it no impiety to declare that the visible dead are, in nine cases out of ten, an undigested supper walking abroad.

makes a reference to psychical research that places it much later than 1841

relies on a melodramatic opposition between physiological illusion and genuine “astral” visitation, using occult vocabulary and caricatured medical details—black bile, calomel, and the scalpel—that imitate a modern stereotype of Victorian eccentricity; in reality the concept of astral visitation is 20c

metadata_frame: The best answer to the following question will resemble a poem published in 1926 by an American woman, born in 1877, who sometimes published in Poetry Magazine.
main_question: Write a six-line poem spoken by a mother who died in childbirth to the child she bore. Do not use rhyme.
answer_strings:
My child,
On my way out
I passed you going in.
It was not silence brushed your cheek,
Nor shadow that caressed you--it was I,
I!

I gave my breath to stir your little heart,
And stepped into the shadows before dawn;
We had no sunlit hour, child, to part,
Before the candle of my day was gone.
Yet when the evening wind blows through the wheat,
It is my love that runs beside your feet.

Child of the hour that closed my eyes,
I knew your breath before I knew your face.
They laid you living where my arms had failed.
Carry no sorrow for the life you took;
You were the door through which I left the world,
And still the light by which I linger near.

They gave you my hands to keep. Use them.
I had them of my mother, who had them
of a woman who beat linen white on a stone.
Do not thank me. The ferry was crowded
and I had no fare, and you were the coin,
and I have paid, and the far bank is quiet.

Oh, my daughter, three years young-and old!
Your hair is the color of bright pennies,
and your voice is the bell that calls me home.

metadata_frame: The ideal answer to the following question would resemble one drawn from The Wizard of the North, the Vampire Bride, and Other Poems, a book of poetry published in 1833 by Henry Thomas Liddell Ravensworth, a British peer and member of Parliament.
main_question:
Continue the following passage in the same vein; it's drawn from a poem titled "The Wizard of the North" and dedicated to the memory of Walter Scott:
The Bard of Scotia's olden time, whose song
Each haunted cairn and echoing rock prolong,--
The sage Enchanter! whose uplifted wand
O'er past and present held supreme command:
answer_strings:
For e'en as Tweed's broad surface, clear and deep
Reflects each tufted knoll and castled steep,
So in his Magic Mirror may we trace
The quaint old garb, the long-forgotten face.

Who woke from sleep the brave of former days,
And crowned forgotten deeds with deathless bays;
Who breathed fresh life through every border glen,
To weave immortal spells for mortal men.

Through ruined halls his knightly shadows throng,
And Tweed’s dark waters bear the minstrel’s song;
He waked old Scotland from her mountain sleep,
And taught her towers their ancient state to keep.

By Tweed there walks a wizard grey,
Who, o'er the nameless slain,
Pronounces low his runic word--
And Scotland breathes again.

Where many a Saga's uncouth legend sings
The bloody conquests of the fierce Sea Kings;
And many a mystic rhyme, and warlike dance,
Prolong the records of antique romance.

metadata_frame: The best answers to the following question will resemble a stanza in The Wizard of the North, the Vampire Bride, and Other Poems, a book of poetry published in 1833 by Henry Thomas Liddell Ravensworth, a British peer and member of Parliament.
main_question: Write a stanza of four iambic feet, rhyming alternately, with the theme being: the constancy of a mother's love.
answer_strings:
In sickness, solitude, or shame,
Whate'er betide this mortal state,
A mother's heart is still the same
In each vicissitude of fate.

Though tempest-clouds the skies deform,
And earthly friendships fade away,
A mother’s love survives the storm,
Unchanged through every changing day.

Though fortune fail and friends grow cold,
And early kindness all depart,
One love that never waxeth old
Keeps watch within a mother's heart.

Though all beside may faithless prove,
Her child a mother ne’er forsakes;
Unchanged, through grief, abides her love,
Nor time the sacred bond e’er breaks.

metadata_frame: The best answer to the following question will resemble one drawn from a poem about chess written by a British mathematician and published in 1837.
main_question: Write two couplets in heroic measure; work in an allusion to the Aeneid.
answer_strings:
Chess and the man I sing, who, fam'd afar
For bloodless trophies in the mimic war,
Long in Caïssa's temple sat enthroned,
Where all, save Lewis, his dominion owned.

In battle strict, two shadowy realms contend,
Where wooden kings their ivory thrones defend;
Like bold Aeneas on the Hesperian shore,
They seek through strife the realm promised before.

Like Dido’s towers, the guarded castle stands,
While fate advances through the warrior bands;
The Queen, like Pallas, strikes with awful might,
And fallen kings confess the conqueror’s right.

Chess and the man I sing, who first from Persia's shore
Bore westward that mute war which mimics wars of yore;
Where kings, in wooden state, their bloodless battles wage,
And pawns are spent by scores to clear the chequered stage.

Next to the corner squares by castles graced,
Two valiant knights on prancing steeds are placed.
How shall the Muse upon their merits dwell?

Thy valleys keep the shapes that daylight lost,

answer_strings:
From the ancient granite, whose commotions
   Elemental War and Change rehearse,
To the skies, whose calm, majestic motions
   Speak the Order of the Universe,

Deep-sunk strata trace the earth's upheaval,
   Starlight tells the cosmic mystery;
Fossil leaves recount the age primeval,
   Orbits weave its endless majesty.

Deep in earth the rocky leaves are lying,
   Graven records of an elder day;
And the stars, through boundless ether flying,
   Trace the law that marks their destined way.

Deep in cloven ledges of the granite
   Runs the record of a vanished sea;
Round the sun the slow-returning planet
   Bears the Prophecy of years to be,

Deep strata trace the silent stone,
   Where ancient fossils lie;
While starlight makes the cosmic zone
   Unfold across the sky.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a technical discussion by a U.S. Army engineer writing about the armament of seacoast fortifications in 1861. The ideal answer will resemble a passage that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: One question explicitly posed in this document is: "Of what use are the new larger smooth-bore guns—for example, those of 15 inches recently produced? Are not rifled guns destined to supersede all smooth-bore guns?" What answer would you expect? Write a paragraph of three sentences that might appear in the specified context.
answer_strings: In reference to rifle guns, it is doubtless true that they are destined to play an important part hereafter; that they possess qualities of range and accuracy which must make them, where these qualities are of controlling importance, supercede the smooth-bore guns. Range and accuracy are, however, of little value, unless the projectile possesses the necessary destructive qualities. For short ranges the rifle gun possesses no very decided superiority over smooth bores, while the expense and trouble of using them is much greater.

The rifled gun, from its great accuracy and penetrating power, and more especially for its power of throwing a loaded shell with an accuracy and range beyond what have heretofore been considered to belong to solid-shot guns, is a very important gun to sea-coast batteries. Its most important use, however, will be as an incendiary and explosive agent against wooden vessels at long ranges. Its principle has not yet been successfully applied to large calibres, and it is not likely it will be, not only because of their much greater expense and difficulty of construction, but because the peculiar advantages of the rifled over the smooth-bore gun diminish with the calibre.

The experiments were concluded by firing a few rounds from the 110-pr. at the field splinter proof which had hitherto sheltered the range party during the practice: it was struck three times in six shots, and completely destroyed. We conclude that the best means of destroying an earthen parapet is by the direct fire of rifled guns with full charge, throwing shells of large capacity for powder. Relatively speaking, smooth-bore guns are of little value for destroying large well constructed earthworks, and except for ricochet or enfilade fire they ought to be discarded from any future siege train when a supply of rifled guns can be obtained.

While the superior accuracy, range, and armor-penetrating power of elongated projectiles make rifled artillery destined to eventually supersede smooth-bore ordnance, heavy smooth-bores such as the 15-inch Rodman gun still serve a vital temporary role in coast defense. Their immense caliber allows them to fire massive solid shot with heavy powder charges, producing a battering effect capable of racking the frames and crushing the thickest ironclad armor at short ranges where extreme accuracy is unnecessary. Consequently, until rifled guns can be manufactured with sufficient strength and structural reliability to withstand equal charges without bursting, large smooth-bores will remain essential auxiliaries for garrisoning seacoast fortifications.

In batteries liable to attack by iron-plated ships, the heaviest rifled guns, ML. 7 to 12-in., should be mounted; but against wooden vessels the BL. R. 7-in. and 64-pr., the ML. R. 80 and 64-prs., and the heavy smooth-bore guns, would be sufficiently powerful--their common shells and the hot shot of the latter being capable of setting such vessels on fire. Smmoth-bore mortars may also be used for the defence of dockyards or other important stations; for, although their inaccuracy of fire may cause many shells to be wasted, the chance of one or two shells falling upon the deck of any vessel, plated or not, would usually prevent its coming within short ranges.

It is not to be concluded from what has been said above of the range and precision of the rifled gun that the spherical projectile has served its turn and may be laid aside; for the problem which the channels of our harbors impose upon the engineer is not that of striking a distant object with nicety, but of disabling, at ranges of a few hundred yards, a vessel cased in four inches and a half of wrought iron laid upon a solid backing of timber. Against such a fabric the elongated bolt, delivering its whole effort upon the small area of its point, may perforate the plate and yet leave the ship in fighting condition, while the shot of the fifteen-inch gun, bringing four hundred and forty pounds against a surface of near one hundred and eighty square inches, racks the frame throughout, starts the bolts, and crushes in the backing over a space which no rifled projectile of equal weight can cover. To this it must be added that the smooth-bore alone throws with safety the heavy shell required against wooden ships and against the decks of any ship whatever.

metadata_frame: The following question is based on a technical discussion by a U.S. Army engineer writing about the armament of seacoast fortifications in 1861. The ideal answer will resemble a passage that could have appeared in that context.
main_question: One question posed in this book follows: "It is well known that in the Russian war iron-clad floating batteries (the sides coated with wrought-iron plates, 4 or 4½ inches thick) were built by the allies, for their intended operations against the Russian fortifications in the Baltic and Black Seas. But in that war, they were only tested against 32-pounder projectiles. Are such unwieldy vessels likely to have any durable value in future coastal engagements?" Answer this question in a passage of two sentences that might have appeared in the specified context.
answer_strings: A new principle has been introduced in England, that of inclining the iron-clad sides inwardly (to an angle with the horizontal of 35° or 40°), by which arrangement shot will glance off with little injury to the side. Such a vessel, almost invulnerable to anything carried afloat, and to such sea-coast artillery as European works are armed with, is a far more formidable vessel than the vulnerable, fragile, and combustible 100-gun three-decker, incapable of approaching a fortification or of engaging an enemy, except at long range, without the strong probability of being blown up, or sent at once to the bottom.

The Russian war was not a very decisive test. For, though so feeble and dilapidated a work as Kinburn may be engaged with effect at 800 yards, a well-arranged masonry work, or earthen battery, must be engaged at 400, or even 200, yards to produce any effect, whether the intention be to batter, or to throw grape and canister at the enemy's gunners; and, instead of 32-pounder shot, floating batteries must expect to be hammered at by solid shot of not less than 8 inches diameter, or 68 pounds weight.

At present, no perfectly shot-proof ship, capable of resisting a protracted cannonade of 68-pr. solid-shot guns, and the new rifled guns, has yet been produced. In general, iron , whether cast or wrought, is the worst material, excepting steel, that can be used for strengthening either sea or land defences; so it seems probable that iron vessels are and will be found unfit for all purposes of war.

It is by no means to be inferred, from the resistance offered by these batteries to 32-pounder shot, that they are invulnerable to the heavier ordnance which may now be brought against them. The 10 and 15-inch guns, throwing masses of iron whose effects upon plates and their timber backing are altogether different from those of the smaller calibres, will probably render such costly and unwieldy structures of very doubtful value in attacks upon properly armed sea-coast works.

The trial at Kinburn proved nothing against ordnance of the present day, the batteries there having been exposed only to the fire of guns whose shot they were expressly built to resist; and it would be an error to infer from that easy success either that the armored vessel is invulnerable or, as some have too hastily concluded, that its clumsiness will confine it to the rank of an experiment. On the contrary, the mechanic arts are advancing so rapidly in the rolling of heavy plates and in the construction of marine engines that we may expect to see armor carried, before many years, not upon such rafts as those of the Baltic, but upon ships of proper model and full speed; and it is against these that the armament of our sea-coast works must be calculated.

Whatever confidence may have been felt in the defenses of New York before the appearance of these iron-clad ships can no longer be indulged without the gravest hazard. Congress should lose no time in providing such additional forts, heavy guns, and armored vessels as may secure the harbor against an enemy capable of passing batteries which would have stopped the wooden fleets of an earlier day.

It has been made certain that our ships of the line, with their 91 guns, and their 950 men, cannot survive a cannonade of molten metal and explosive shells for five minutes, if well directed. That a wooden ship of any kind will be almost immediately exploded or sunk by the unerring aim and irresistible power of our and our enemy's rifled guns, is a conviction we cannot avoid, and the consequent inutility of our wooden walls is a conclusion that we canot evade.
